items.x: The idea comes from Gillian Hadfield and Jack Clark, who propose that governments require regulated companies to buy oversight services from government-licensed private regulators, so market incentives develop the technical methods while government sets priorities. California's SB 813 (signed September 9, 2026) borrows part of the idea in voluntary form: a state agency designates independent verification organizations (IVOs) and can suspend or end a designation.

choice.p: What is the core argument for having government certify private AI safety verifiers?
o: Private verifiers adapt faster, while government sets the goals and polices them
Private verifiers can legally block model releases, which government agencies cannot do
It lets each lab set its own safety goals, with no government involvement at all
It replaces lawsuits as the only way to hold AI developers accountable
ow: Government agencies can also hold power to block releases, as under licensing; the case for verifiers rests on expertise and speed.
Government sets the goals in this model; labs don't choose their own standards.
These proposals leave lawsuits in place; some make verification count in court.

items.p: What do supporters say a license to build or release frontier AI models can do that disclosure rules and liability can't?
items.answer: Act before harm. Disclosure and liability work after the fact, while a license lets government stop a dangerous model before it is built or shipped, and the threat of losing a license gives the regulator strong leverage over a few high-value companies.
keys: stops dangerous models before training or release
disclosure and liability act after the fact
the threat of revocation gives leverage
items.x: The strongest versions make the license depend on meeting safety standards and passing review, with the power to revoke it. The 2023 Blumenthal-Hawley framework proposed licensing by an independent oversight body; Sen. Bernie Sanders's Ban Artificial Superintelligence Act (2026) would require a federal charter to develop advanced models and approval before each deployment.

choice.p: What do supporters say licensing can do that disclosure rules and liability cannot?
o: Stop a dangerous model before anyone builds or releases it
Make developers pay compensation after an AI system has harmed someone
Let the public read each lab's safety plans, test results and incident reports
Check once a year whether each lab follows the safety plan it published
ow: Compensating victims after the fact is what liability does.
Public visibility into safety plans is what disclosure rules provide.
Checking adherence to a lab's own plan is a third-party audit.

items.p: Why do supporters argue a dedicated frontier AI regulator is needed even if audits, testing and certified verifiers exist?
items.answer: Every other tool needs someone with expertise and authority to run it. US frontier oversight is spread across voluntary CAISI testing, state attorneys general and agencies with no AI mandate, so no one can act quickly. A dedicated body could keep thresholds current, build technical staff and enforce rules consistently.
keys: other tools need an institution to run and enforce them
oversight is fragmented; no one has both expertise and authority
could update rules, build staff and enforce consistently
items.x: Designs range from a new agency to an office inside an existing one. New York put its RAISE Act office (called DIGIT) inside the Department of Financial Services, and the EU's AI Office gained powers to enforce its rules for general-purpose AI models on August 2, 2026.

choice.p: What gap do supporters say a dedicated frontier AI regulator would fill?
o: No US body has the expertise and power to oversee frontier AI
No federal agency currently tests frontier models for dangerous capabilities at all
Courts have no power to hear lawsuits over harms caused by AI systems
No state requires frontier AI labs to publish any safety information
ow: CAISI already tests models, though only voluntarily.
Courts can hear AI-related lawsuits under existing law.
California's SB 53 already requires large developers to publish safety frameworks.

items.p: Some proposals would require agencies to log officials' AI use and keep the logs as public records, open to Freedom of Information Act (FOIA) requests and auditors. According to supporters, what failure would this prevent?
items.answer: As officials use AI to draft rules and make decisions, the prompts and outputs may be the only record of how a decision was made. And AI could let a few people run large parts of government without the many staff who might refuse or leak. Reviewable logs let Congress, courts, auditors and the public see and deter misuse.
keys: AI interactions may be the only record of how decisions were made
AI could remove the check of staff who would refuse
logs let outsiders review and deter misuse
items.x: Stefan Torges of Forethought warns that "as AI replaces humans in government, nobody will be left to refuse" unlawful orders. He proposes comprehensive logging of government AI use, with the logs designated federal records, plus more capacity for the Government Accountability Office (GAO) to audit AI in national security.

choice.p: What failure are proposals to log government officials' AI use as public records meant to prevent?
o: AI-assisted decisions leave no record, and AI could replace staff who'd refuse or leak
Agencies buy AI tools from vendors without competitive bidding or price checks
Officials' AI chats expose citizens' personal data to the vendors that run them
Agencies rely on models that haven't passed any dangerous-capability tests
ow: Procurement rules address how agencies buy AI; logging addresses how they use it.
Privacy is a real concern with AI chats, but records proposals aim to preserve interactions for review.
Testing models before use is a separate tool; logs record what officials do with them.

items.p: Under voluntary certified-verifier designs, developers don’t have to get verified. What do these designs offer developers as a reason to opt in?
items.answer: Help in court. If the developer is later sued over harms, having passed verification can count in its defense, ranging from evidence that counts but doesn't decide the case (SB 813 as enacted) to a full defense against liability in some proposals.
keys: a benefit in later lawsuits or liability protection
works as an incentive in place of a mandate
items.x: As enacted in September 2026, SB 813 says an audit done under the state's standards is "relevant to, but not conclusive of" a lawsuit over AI harms. Its 2025 version went further, offering certified developers an affirmative defense. Not every verifier design is voluntary: Hadfield and Clark's original "regulatory markets" idea would require companies to buy oversight, and the federal FRONTIER Act bill would require the very largest developers to retain a licensed verifier.

choice.p: In voluntary certified-verifier (IVO) designs like California's SB 813, what draws developers to opt in?
o: Legal protection or favorable weight if they are later sued over harms
An exemption from every state AI safety law that would otherwise apply
Permission to skip government safety testing before each release
A waiver from having to publish their safety frameworks
ow: Broad exemptions from state laws come from federal preemption, a separate fight.
IVO proposals don't waive pre-release testing; they add a separate check.
Verification builds on published frameworks; it doesn't waive them.

items.p: A statutory duty of care would require frontier AI developers to take reasonable care to avoid causing or enabling catastrophic harm, enforced through lawsuits. What failure do supporters say it addresses?
items.answer: Commercial and competitive pressure pushes labs to skip safety work, while much of the harm their models could cause would fall on other people. Legal exposure for careless conduct makes those precautions effectively mandatory, so lawyers and boards treat them as required.
keys: competitive or commercial pressure leads labs to skip safety work
much of the harm would fall on others, so labs underinvest in precautions
legal exposure makes precautions effectively mandatory
items.x: 'Reasonable care' is the negligence standard: a developer is liable only if it failed to act as a careful developer would and that failure caused the harm. Gabriel Weil says liability puts 'a thumb on the other side of the scale' against labs' financial incentives to push ahead. California's vetoed SB 1047 (2024) would have let the state attorney general sue developers that failed to comply.

choice.p: What failure do supporters say a statutory duty of care for frontier developers addresses?
o: Labs under competitive pressure skip safety work whose harms would fall on others
Victims of AI harms cannot tell which company built the model that hurt them
Developers cannot pay for huge harms, so their victims go uncompensated
Employees who spot dangers stay silent for fear of retaliation by the lab
ow: That is a tracing problem; a duty of care assumes the developer is known.
That is the 'judgment-proof' problem that insurance mandates target.
That is the gap whistleblower protections target.

items.p: Why do supporters of a duty of care prefer a general 'reasonable care' standard to a detailed list of required safety practices written into law?
items.answer: It is flexible: courts can judge new or unforeseen harm pathways (such as internal deployment, weak security of model weights or open release) case by case, so lawmakers don't have to anticipate every risk in advance.
keys: flexible standard
courts judge new or unforeseen harm pathways case by case
lawmakers don't need to anticipate every risk in advance
items.x: Legal scholar Ketan Ramakrishnan offers a qualified defense of negligence for foundation models, arguing that only it is broad enough to reach pathways like internal deployment, weak model-weight security and open-source release. He also proposes that courts, without any statute, widen the duty of care to cover AI behavior that would break important laws or norms if a human did it.

choice.p: Why do supporters of a duty of care prefer a general 'reasonable care' standard to a detailed list of required safety practices?
o: Courts judge new harm pathways case by case, so lawmakers needn't foresee every risk
It makes developers pay for all harms, even after taking every precaution
It gives developers a clear checklist of practices that guarantees immunity from lawsuits
It moves enforcement from the courts to a new federal AI safety agency
ow: That describes strict liability; under negligence, a developer that took reasonable care is not liable.
That describes a safe harbor; a general standard is less predictable than a checklist.
A duty of care is enforced mainly through courts and attorneys general.

items.p: Product-liability proposals would let people harmed by an AI system sue its developer over a defective design or missing warnings. How do supporters say exposure to these lawsuits makes AI safer?
items.answer: Developers expect to pay for harms their systems cause others, so they have a financial reason to invest in safer design, testing and warnings before release. The developer, who knows the system best, chooses which precautions to take, so no regulator has to specify them.
keys: developers bear the cost of harms they cause others
financial reason to invest in safer design, testing and warnings
the developer chooses the precautions; no regulator has to specify them
items.x: Economists call this internalizing an externality: making whoever creates a risk pay its costs. Sen. Dick Durbin said his AI LEAD Act 'will force AI companies to develop their products with safety in mind.'

choice.p: How do supporters say letting people sue AI developers over defective products makes AI safer?
o: Developers expect to pay for harms, so they invest in safer design
Lawsuits give regulators the evidence they need to license each model
Court settlements fund a public agency that inspects AI developers
Developers must buy insurance, and their insurers then inspect the labs
ow: Product liability works through private lawsuits; it creates no licensing system.
Damages go to injured people; funding an agency is a different policy.
That describes an insurance mandate, a separate tool often paired with liability.

items.p: Some proposals would require frontier developers to carry liability insurance or other financial assurance sized to the harm their models could cause. Name two things supporters say this adds to liability alone.
items.answer: (1) Victims get paid even when the harm exceeds what the developer can pay (it is 'judgment-proof'), which keeps liability credible. (2) Premiums put a price on risk before harm occurs, so riskier models cost more to deploy. (3) Insurers monitor developers, demand safety practices and lobby for stricter rules. (4) A model could be deployed only if someone will insure it.
keys: pays victims even when the developer can't (judgment-proof)
keeps liability credible for very large harms
premiums price risk, so riskier models cost more to deploy
insurers monitor developers and demand safety practices
deployment depends on finding an insurer
items.x: 'Judgment-proof' means a defendant can't pay what a court awards, so the threat of liability loses force. Cristian Trout argues insurers would model risk, monitor developers, lobby for stricter rules and advise on preventing losses. Gabriel Weil suggests a regulator could set required coverage by the worst harm a system might cause, so a model deploys only if an insurer will write an affordable policy.

choice.p: What do supporters say an insurance mandate adds to liability alone?
o: Victims get paid even if the developer can't, and insurers police safety
Developers get a legal shield from all lawsuits once they buy a qualifying insurance policy
A government fund replaces private lawsuits as the way victims are compensated
Insurers take over writing the safety rules that regulators would otherwise set
ow: Insurance pays claims; victims can still sue.
Mandates rely on private insurers; a government fund is a different design.
Insurers influence safety through pricing and policy conditions; they gain no rulemaking power.

items.p: A liability safe harbor protects a developer from some lawsuits if it meets set conditions, such as publishing a safety plan or passing a certified audit. Why do supporters prefer this to safety mandates or ordinary lawsuits?
items.answer: It uses legal certainty as a reward: firms adopt safety practices voluntarily to earn protection, which supporters say spreads good practice faster than mandates, rewards firms that accept outside verification, and spares them inconsistent standards set by many different juries.
keys: legal certainty works as a reward for adopting safety practices
spreads good practice faster or more flexibly than mandates
rewards accepting outside verification
avoids inconsistent standards from many juries
items.x: 'Safe harbor' is a legal term for conditions that, if met, protect you from a penalty or lawsuit. It can be full immunity, a defense the developer raises in court, or a presumption that it met the standard of care. Dean Ball has proposed government-certified private auditors, with a liability safe harbor as one possible reward for certified labs.

choice.p: Why do supporters prefer a liability safe harbor to safety mandates or ordinary lawsuits?
o: Firms adopt safety practices to earn legal certainty, without rigid mandates
It raises the damages for AI harms, so firms fear lawsuits more than they do now
It lets labs coordinate release pauses without facing antitrust lawsuits
It moves all AI lawsuits into a single specialized federal court
ow: A safe harbor reduces liability exposure; it does not raise damages.
That describes an antitrust safe harbor, which shields coordination from competition law.
Safe harbors set conditions for protection; they don't change which court hears cases.

items.p: What gap do supporters say AI whistleblower protections close?
items.answer: Lab employees are often the first to see dangerous capabilities, skipped safety tests or misleading public statements, but contracts and fear of retaliation can keep them quiet. Protection makes it safer to tell regulators or Congress, giving government a window into labs without building a large new agency.
keys: insiders see problems first
contracts or retaliation keep them silent
gives government visibility into labs
items.x: In May 2024, Vox reported that OpenAI's exit paperwork tied departing employees' vested equity to signing a non-disparagement clause; OpenAI then removed the clause and released former employees from it. California's SB 53 has protected covered frontier-lab employees who report catastrophic risks since Jan. 1, 2026.

choice.p: What gap do supporters say AI whistleblower protections close?
o: Insiders who see dangers first can be silenced by contracts or fear of retaliation
Developers can't pay for huge harms, which leaves their victims uncompensated
Rival labs can't legally agree to slow down together, even for safety
Courts lack the technical experts needed to judge AI lawsuits fairly
ow: That is the gap insurance mandates target.
That is the gap an antitrust safe harbor targets.
Court expertise is a real issue, but whistleblower laws don't address it.

items.p: Antitrust law generally bars competitors from agreeing to limit their products. Why do some people propose an antitrust safe harbor for AI safety coordination?
items.answer: So labs can share security threat information and agree to slow or delay training or releases for safety without risking an illegal-collusion lawsuit. Without it, no lab wants to slow down alone, and a joint slowdown could be treated as a cartel.
keys: lets labs share safety or security threat information
lets labs agree to slow or delay for safety
without it, joint slowdowns could count as illegal collusion
no lab wants to slow down alone
items.x: Supporters describe a collective-action problem: each lab may prefer that everyone slow down, but none will slow down alone. In September 2026, Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei called for industry-wide coordination to 'pace the frontier' and suggested some of it might need waivers of antitrust restrictions.

choice.p: Why do some people propose an antitrust safe harbor for AI safety coordination?
o: So labs can share threat data and slow releases without collusion suits
So labs can pool customer data to train safer models without facing privacy suits
So the government can force rival labs to merge into one national AI project
So labs can set common prices to help fund the cost of their safety research
ow: Proposals cover security-risk information; pooling customer data raises separate privacy issues.
A safe harbor permits voluntary coordination; it forces nothing.
Price-fixing stays illegal under proposals such as the CATS Act.

items.p: Some reformers want frontier labs legally bound to a public mission through nonprofit control, independent trusts or mission-bound boards, with state attorneys general enforcing it. What failure are these structures meant to prevent?
items.answer: If a lab's board answers only to investors, commercial pressure wins close calls about training, releasing and using the most capable systems. Mission-locked governance puts a body with no stake in profits between the lab and that pressure, and attorney general oversight adds outside enforcement.
keys: boards answerable only to investors let profit win close safety calls
a body with no profit stake checks those decisions
attorneys general enforce the mission from outside
items.x: This tool works through corporate and charity law, since whoever controls a frontier lab decides how its systems are trained and released. A public benefit corporation (PBC) is a for-profit company whose charter requires its board to weigh a stated public mission alongside profits.

choice.p: What failure are mission-locked lab governance structures, such as nonprofit control or independent trusts, meant to prevent?
o: Investor-only boards letting commercial pressure win close safety calls
Employees leaking model weights to foreign governments for money
Rival labs colluding to raise the prices they charge customers
Regulators lacking the technical expertise to evaluate models
ow: Weight security is a separate problem handled by security standards.
Collusion is an antitrust problem; these structures concern who controls a single lab.
Regulatory capacity is a separate issue; these structures work inside the company.

items.p: Export controls require licenses to sell advanced AI chips and chipmaking tools to China and other countries of concern. How do supporters say this reduces risk from advanced AI?
items.answer: Frontier AI takes huge numbers of advanced chips, and a few U.S. and allied firms control their supply. Restricting that supply slows rivals' frontier development and limits the compute their militaries and labs can use, which supporters say keeps the U.S. and its allies in the lead.
keys: frontier AI needs huge numbers of advanced chips
a few U.S. and allied firms control supply, a chokepoint
slows rivals' frontier development
keeps the U.S. and allies ahead and limits adversary militaries
items.x: Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei argued in January 2025 that the controls keep 'democratic nations at the forefront of AI development.' The Commerce Department's Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) writes the rules under the Export Control Reform Act of 2018. The theory assumes controls hold up against smuggling and cloud rental, and that China can't quickly build substitutes.

choice.p: How do supporters say chip export controls reduce risk from advanced AI?
o: Limiting sales of chips a few U.S. and allied firms control slows rivals and keeps a lead
Tracking where each chip is located lets officials catch chips smuggled to banned buyers
Checking who rents cloud compute lets the government see who is training very large models
Requiring strong security at data centers keeps rivals from stealing trained frontier models
ow: That describes chip location verification, a tool for enforcing export controls after chips are sold.
That describes cloud know-your-customer rules, which cover renting chips remotely.
That describes data center and weight security, which protect models that are already trained.

items.p: Some proposals add location verification to AI chips. What is it meant to accomplish?
items.answer: In the near term, catching smuggling and diversion of export-controlled chips, which current enforcement misses. In the longer run, a technical base for verifying compliance with international compute limits without trusting the other side.
keys: catch smuggling or diversion of controlled chips
current enforcement misses much diversion
could verify international compute agreements
items.x: Narrow versions only estimate roughly which country a chip is in, using signal delays; broader proposals would also verify what chips are used for.

choice.p: What are chip location verification requirements meant to accomplish?
o: Catch chip smuggling now, and later help verify international compute limits
Let the government switch off any chip remotely as soon as it is misused anywhere in the world
Show regulators which cloud customers are renting chips to train the largest AI models
Stop hackers and insiders from copying model weights out of data centers
ow: Remote disable is a stronger, more opposed proposal; location checks only report roughly where a chip is.
That is the job of cloud know-your-customer rules.
That is the job of model weight and data center security standards.

items.p: Why do proposals require cloud providers that rent out AI chips to know their customers?
items.answer: Export controls restrict sales of advanced chips, but companies in restricted countries can rent the same chips through cloud data centers. Know-your-customer rules aim to let the government see who is training very large models and deny service to adversaries.
keys: closes the cloud-rental gap in export controls
lets government see who trains very large models
can deny service to adversaries
items.x: Commerce proposed a customer identification rule for cloud (infrastructure-as-a-service) providers in January 2024, which would also have required reports on foreign customers whose transactions could help train large AI models. Supporters Janet Egan and Lennart Heim describe compute as 'emerging as a node for oversight' of frontier AI.

choice.p: Why do proposals require cloud providers that rent out AI chips to know their customers?
o: Restricted firms can rent controlled chips through the cloud, so providers check who rents
Cloud data centers are the easiest place for hackers to steal trained model weights
Chips installed in cloud data centers are often smuggled abroad later without anyone noticing
Cloud providers run most open-weight models, so tracking renters stops their spread
ow: That is the concern behind data center and model weight security standards.
Smuggling is what chip location verification targets.
KYC is about who rents compute for training; open-weight policy is a separate debate.

items.p: Why do proposals to prevent theft of frontier models attach security requirements to AI data centers in particular?
items.answer: Frontier model weights and secrets are stored and used in data centers, so a breach there could undo other safeguards. Builders also need things government controls, such as grid connections, land and permits, so security can be made a condition of those benefits. Supporters say this fixes a market failure: labs racing each other underinvest in security.
keys: weights and secrets are stored and used there
a breach there undoes other safeguards
builders need grid power, land or permits from government
security can be made a condition of those benefits
racing labs underinvest in security on their own
items.x: IFP's 2025 'Compute in America' playbook proposed tying federal energy and permitting help, including sites on federal land, to security requirements, arguing that labs that spend enough to stop Chinese state hackers risk falling behind rivals. The approach assumes standards can reach nation-state level in time and that builders don't move abroad.

choice.p: Why do proposals to prevent theft of frontier models attach security requirements to AI data centers in particular?
o: Model weights sit there, and builders need grid power, land and permits, giving leverage
Data centers store users' chat histories, so the rules mainly protect consumer privacy
Data centers are where export-controlled chips are most often smuggled out of the country
Data centers are where cloud customers' identities are checked before they can rent chips
ow: Privacy laws apply too, but these proposals aim to stop rival states stealing or sabotaging frontier models.
Smuggling is the target of chip location verification.
Checking renters is the job of cloud know-your-customer rules.

items.p: Why do security proposals treat theft of a frontier model's weights as such a serious risk?
items.answer: Weights are the product of very costly training. Whoever steals them can run the model cheaply without the developer's safeguards or monitoring, and spread it. That hands a rival the payoff of the training, speeding up a race, and undoes other controls such as export controls or deployment limits.
keys: weights embody very costly training
a thief can run the model without safeguards or monitoring, and spread it
rivals skip costly training, speeding a race
undoes other controls (export controls, deployment limits)
items.x: RAND's 2024 report says that once attackers have the weights, abusing the model without restrictions is 'eminently feasible,' needing only computing power to run it. Its recommendations for labs include keeping all copies of weights on a few monitored systems and cutting the number of people with access.

choice.p: Why do security proposals treat theft of a frontier model's weights as such a serious risk?
o: A thief can run the model without safeguards and skip costly training, undoing other controls
Stolen weights would expose the private data and chat histories of everyone who has used the model
Stolen weights would let attackers take control of the lab's data centers
Weights hold the only record of a model's safety tests, which regulators rely on
ow: Weights are learned parameters; the main worry is a rival running the model itself.
Weights are a model file; stealing them doesn't give control of any facility.
Test records are separate documents; weights are what make the model run.

items.p: Why do some safety advocates want limits on publishing the weights of the most capable models?
items.answer: Once weights are public, anyone can fine-tune the safeguards away, and the release can't be recalled. So if a model has dangerous capabilities, such as meaningful help with cyberattacks or bioweapons, open release hands them to everyone permanently.
keys: fine-tuning can strip safeguards
a release can't be recalled
dangerous capabilities become available to anyone, permanently
items.x: Elizabeth Seger and co-authors argued in 2023 that some highly capable models should not be open-sourced, at least at first. FAR.AI researchers showed in 2025 that fine-tuning, through open weights or closed fine-tuning services, can produce models that help with harmful requests. Capability-threshold proposals would restrict only models above a dangerous-capability line.

choice.p: Why do some safety advocates want limits on publishing the weights of the most capable models?
o: Fine-tuning can strip safeguards from published weights, and a release can't be recalled
Published weights reveal the private data that was used to train the model
Open models are always more capable than the closed models they compete with
Publishing weights lets anyone see which chips were used and evade export controls
ow: Weights are learned parameters; the worry is what the model can do once anyone can modify it.
Capability varies by model; the concern applies only to the most capable ones.
Export controls cover chips; the worry about weights is removing safeguards.

items.p: Why do biosecurity proposals focus on screening DNA synthesis orders, rather than only on AI models?
items.answer: Turning a pathogen design into a weapon still requires physical DNA, and DNA synthesis is a narrow industry. Screening orders and customers there is a chokepoint that works no matter which AI model produced the design, including openly released ones.
keys: designs still need physical DNA
synthesis is a concentrated chokepoint
works regardless of which model was used, including open-weight models
items.x: The researchers behind a 2025 Science study on screening describe DNA synthesis as 'a choke point' in AI-assisted protein engineering. Proposals pair checks on orders with checks that customers are legitimate.

choice.p: Why do biosecurity proposals focus on screening DNA synthesis orders, rather than only on AI models?
o: Designs need physical DNA from a narrow industry, so screening covers any model
AI models can't meaningfully help with biology, so rules on models would have no effect
DNA synthesis companies run most of the AI biology models, so they are easiest to regulate
Screening shows which cloud customers are training biology models on rented chips overseas
ow: Proposals assume AI may lower barriers in biology; screening complements rules on models.
DNA synthesis companies make DNA; AI design tools are built and run by others.
That would be cloud know-your-customer; screening checks DNA orders and buyers.

items.p: A kill switch mandate requires large AI companies to keep a tested ability to halt, restrict or shut down their AI systems. What failure is it meant to handle, and why do supporters want the capability required in advance?
items.answer: A deployed or internally used model that starts causing serious harm (for example a loss-of-control incident or a cyberattack) faster than the company could improvise a response. Requiring the capability in advance means a tested off-switch covering the whole deployment already exists when it is needed.
keys: a model causing serious harm, such as loss of control
harm moves faster than an improvised response
a tested switch already exists when it is needed
items.x: The Lieu-Moran AI Kill Switch Act (H.R. 9917, July 2026) would require the ability to stop inference, cut off user access, suspend specific accounts and fully shut down. After a defined incident, DHS could order proportionate action, from a slowdown up to shutdown, and DHS must consider also requiring graduated options such as throttling or switching to an earlier model version. As of October 2026, the federal bills were still in committee and California had only ordered expert recommendations.

choice.p: What failure is a kill switch mandate mainly meant to handle?
o: A model causing serious harm with no ready way to stop it
A developer that refuses to stop a model the government judges imminently dangerous
A race in which no lab wants to be the first to stop at a dangerous threshold
An AI agent that causes harm when no one can tell who built or runs it
ow: That is the gap emergency halt authority fills: a legal power to override the developer. A kill switch mandate is about having the technical means to stop.
That is the problem conditional pauses target, by agreeing on a trigger in advance.
That is the problem agent identification and logging target.

items.p: Most frontier AI rules require disclosure and leave the decision to deploy with the developer. What gap is a government emergency halt power meant to fill?
items.answer: The case where a specific model clearly poses an imminent catastrophic risk and the developer won't stop it. The power gives an official (or a court) a legal way to quickly suspend or restrict that model's development, deployment or internal use.
keys: a model posing imminent catastrophic risk
the developer won't stop on its own
a legal power to suspend or restrict it quickly
items.x: Commentators such as Dean Ball argue that a law passed by Congress could also put guardrails on improvised government action, such as the June 2026 export-control halt of two Anthropic models. In the EU, the AI Act lets the European Commission request that a provider restrict, withdraw or recall a general-purpose AI model, a power that applies from Aug. 2, 2026.

choice.p: What gap is a government emergency halt power mainly meant to fill?
o: A clearly dangerous model whose developer won't stop it
A model that can't be stopped because its company never built an off-switch
AI agents whose owners can't be identified after they cause harm
Local electricity price rises caused by large new AI data centers
ow: That is the technical gap a kill switch mandate fills. A halt power is a legal authority to order a stop.
That is the problem agent identification and logging target.
That is the main motive behind local data center moratoria.

items.p: AI agents are AI systems that take actions on their own, such as running code or moving money. What problem are proposals for agent IDs and action logs meant to solve?
items.answer: A harmful or hijacked agent can act across many systems before anyone knows whose it is. An ID tied to the responsible developer or operator, plus logs of its significant actions, makes incidents traceable, so investigators know whom to hold responsible and which specific agent to shut down.
keys: harmful agents are hard to trace to an owner
the ID links an agent to whoever built or runs it
logs record what it did
lets people hold the owner responsible and stop that agent
items.x: Researchers led by Alan Chan (2024) propose IDs for each instance of an AI system, comparing them to identifiers for individual aircraft. Uses they list include checking a system's safety certifications before dealing with it and knowing whom to contact to shut down a malfunctioning one.

choice.p: What problem are AI agent IDs and action logs mainly meant to solve?
o: No one can tell whose a harmful agent is or what it did
Models could be trained past dangerous capability levels before anyone notices
Companies may lack the technical ability to halt their own models
Model weights could be stolen from AI companies by foreign hackers
ow: That is closer to what conditional pauses and capability evaluations target.
That is what kill switch mandates address. IDs help find the right agent to stop.
That is the target of model weight security rules.

items.p: Frontier labs now use their own models to write code and run experiments. Why do supporters of limits on this automated AI R&D (AI systems doing AI research) see it as a special danger?
items.answer: AI improving its own successors (recursive self-improvement) could make progress dramatically faster, leaving too little time to evaluate models, fix safety problems or let governments respond. It could also concentrate power in the company that controls the most capable internal models.
keys: recursive self-improvement could sharply speed progress
too little time for evaluation, safety fixes or government response
could concentrate power in the leading developer
items.x: CSET's January 2026 workshop report calls automated AI R&D a potential source of major strategic surprise and says "This warrants preparatory action now." It notes that public information about it depends almost entirely on patchy, voluntary company disclosures. Dario Amodei warns that, left unchecked, it could "outrun our ability to understand and control these systems."

choice.p: Why do supporters of limits on automated AI R&D see AI doing AI research as a special danger?
o: Progress could outrun safety work and government oversight
It would replace many human AI researchers and push their pay sharply down
AI-written code is more likely to contain security bugs than human-written code
It lets labs train new models without needing any more chips or data centers
ow: Job effects are a real debate, but these policies target progress outrunning oversight.
Code quality matters, but it isn't the reason for pacing or disclosure proposals.
Automated research still uses computing power. The worry is the pace of progress.

items.p: Why do supporters of a legal ban on building superintelligence (AI far more capable than humans across most tasks) argue that a ban is needed, instead of safety rules for how it is built?
items.answer: They argue no one knows how to control a system far smarter than humans, so building one risks human extinction or permanent disempowerment, and rules for building it safely can't remove that risk. The only reliable protection is not building it, at least until the control problem is solved.
keys: no one knows how to control a much smarter system
risk of extinction or permanent disempowerment
the only reliable protection is not building it
items.x: MIRI calls a ban "the only effective solution to avoid the ASI threat, at least in the near term." The Sanders-Casar Ban Artificial Superintelligence Act (Sept. 2026) defines superintelligence as AI that exceeds human performance across most domains, or that could plan and carry out humanity's destruction or disempowerment.

choice.p: Why do supporters of a legal ban on superintelligence argue a ban is needed?
o: No one knows how to control it, so the only reliable protection is not building it
Superintelligence would mainly be used to spread misinformation at huge scale, which a ban would prevent
Courts have already ruled that existing safety laws cannot reach superintelligent systems
A ban is cheaper than a testing regime because it needs no monitoring or inspections at all
ow: Supporters' central worry is losing control of the system itself, up to human extinction.
Supporters' argument rests on the technical problem of controlling a smarter system.
Supporters such as MIRI say a ban needs monitoring, including tracking of AI chips.

items.p: Conditional pauses stop frontier AI training or deployment when a capability or compute threshold is crossed. What problem are they meant to solve, and why do supporters want the trigger agreed in advance?
items.answer: A race: no lab or country wants to stop alone, and the pressure to keep going grows as systems get more powerful. Agreeing on the trigger in advance lets actors commit to stopping before competitive pressure peaks.
keys: racing: no one wants to stop alone
commit before competitive pressure peaks
trigger is a capability or compute threshold
items.x: Versions range from voluntary company if-then commitments to a legal halt above a compute threshold, a verified industry pause, and an international moratorium. Anthropic has said that if verification systems existed, it expects it would slow down or temporarily pause "if other developers at or near the frontier also did so in a verifiable manner."

choice.p: What problem are conditional pauses mainly meant to solve?
o: A race in which no lab or country wants to stop first, even at a dangerous threshold
A developer refusing to stop one specific model the government finds dangerous
A company lacking the technical means to shut down its deployed model
Rising local power bills caused by large new data centers
ow: That is the problem emergency halt authority addresses.
That is the problem kill switch mandates address.
That is the main motive behind local data center moratoria.

items.p: Why can if-then commitments ('if a model has capability X, then safeguard Y must be in place, or development waits') win support from people who disagree about AI risk?
items.answer: Adopting one doesn't require agreeing that dangerous capabilities are coming soon. It only requires agreeing on what would be needed if the capability appeared, so people who expect it soon and people who expect it never can both accept it.
keys: no need to agree that risks are imminent
only agree on what to do if the capability appears
acceptable to people with very different expectations
items.x: Holden Karnofsky (Carnegie Endowment, 2024) makes this argument. His example tripwire is a model able to walk a novice through building a weapon of mass destruction. The 'then' would include making that help hard to get from the model and storing its weights where theft is very unlikely.

choice.p: Why can if-then commitments win support from people who disagree about AI risk?
o: People needn't agree dangers are near, only on what to do if a capability appears
They are enforced by courts, which people on both sides trust more than regulators
They impose no costs on developers until an international AI treaty is signed
They apply only to open-weight models, which people on both sides already distrust
ow: Many if-then commitments are voluntary company policies. Court enforcement isn't the point.
They bite when a capability appears, with no treaty needed.
They apply to any model that reaches the capability.

items.p: Some propose halting the construction of AI data centers nationwide until Congress enacts safeguards, including on AI safety. What AI-safety argument do supporters of a national moratorium make?
items.answer: Frontier AI progress depends on ever larger computing clusters, so withholding new capacity could slow capability growth. Tying the end of the pause to new laws also gives Congress a reason to pass safety rules.
keys: frontier AI needs ever larger computing clusters
less new capacity slows capability growth
lifting the pause depends on passing safeguards
items.x: Rep. Ocasio-Cortez said expansion should stop "until we have a framework to adequately address the existential harm AI poses to our society." The other lifting conditions include protections for workers, electricity prices and the environment. The argument assumes new data centers are the binding limit on progress and that building can't simply move abroad; the bill would also bar exports of AI computing hardware to countries without comparable safeguards.

choice.p: What is the AI-safety argument for a national moratorium on new AI data centers?
o: Withholding new computing capacity could slow frontier progress and push Congress to pass safety rules
Data centers are the main way AI models escape onto the internet, so fewer centers means fewer escapes
A moratorium lets regulators inspect every model trained in existing data centers
Fewer data centers would make AI agents easier to identify and trace
ow: The argument is about slowing growth in computing power; escape risk doesn't depend on how many facilities exist.
A moratorium stops new construction. It doesn't create inspection powers.
Agent identification is a separate tool, unrelated to how many facilities exist.

items.p: Some bills would bar AI from nuclear launch decisions and require human responsibility for every use of force. According to supporters, what failure are these limits meant to prevent?
items.answer: Force, up to nuclear use, applied at machine speed with few humans in the chain. Fewer humans means fewer people who can catch an accident or refuse an illegal or catastrophic order, whether the danger is a malfunction or a small group misusing autonomous forces.
keys: machine-speed force with few humans involved
fewer people to catch accidents, such as AI-triggered nuclear use
fewer people able to refuse illegal or catastrophic orders
items.x: The main vehicle is the annual National Defense Authorization Act (NDAA). The Senate's FY2027 NDAA as reported (S. 4784) would bar the Pentagon from using AI 'for the decision to initiate the launch or detonation of a nuclear weapon' and require rules ensuring that no weapon system will 'eliminate human responsibility for the use of force.' Sen. Kirsten Gillibrand says such decisions 'must always be made by human beings, not unaccountable machines.'

choice.p: According to supporters, statutory limits on military AI mainly guard against which failure?
o: Machines using force with too few humans to catch errors or refuse illegal orders
Adversaries stealing U.S. military AI models and turning them against U.S. forces
The Pentagon becoming locked into one or two AI vendors and overpaying them
Rival militaries fielding autonomous weapons faster than the United States can field its own
ow: That is the concern behind model weight security rules, which protect the models themselves from theft.
That is the concern behind multi-vendor procurement rules, a competition tool.
That worry is usually raised as a reason to speed up military autonomy; these limits aim to keep humans accountable for force.

items.p: What problem is 'law-following AI', meaning government AI built to refuse clearly unlawful orders, meant to address?
items.answer: Coups and abuses of power have historically needed many people's cooperation, and some refuse. If AI replaces those soldiers, analysts and civil servants, that check disappears unless the AI itself will refuse illegal orders.
keys: power grabs need many people's cooperation
AI could replace those people
keeps a refusal check inside the system
items.x: Cullen O'Keefe (Institute for Law & AI) and Ketan Ramakrishnan (Yale Law School) warn that otherwise government agents become 'AI henchmen': loyal to an official, unconstrained by law, and immune to the threat of punishment that deters human subordinates from carrying out illegal orders.

choice.p: What problem is law-following AI, meaning government AI built to refuse clearly unlawful orders, meant to address?
o: AI could replace the people whose refusals check abuses of power
Government AI could make biased decisions about benefits, arrests or visas
Developers could hide dangerous model capabilities from government safety regulators
AI agents could cause harms for which no person can be held legally liable
ow: That is the target of process rules like impact assessments, human review and appeals for high-impact government AI.
That is the target of transparency and reporting rules for developers.
That is the target of liability proposals; law-following AI is about refusing unlawful orders from the AI's own principals.

items.p: Supporters of limits on government AI use in surveillance, policing and immigration enforcement say AI creates a new danger even if no surveillance law changes. What is it?
items.answer: AI makes it cheap to watch, sort and act against huge numbers of people, work that once needed thousands of cooperating staff. That erodes a practical check on abuse. Bans, approval requirements and audits try to restore friction for the most dangerous uses and let courts, Congress and the press see misuse.
keys: cheap surveillance and enforcement at mass scale
it once needed many cooperating staff, a practical check
limits restore friction; logging and audits expose misuse
items.x: Today's government-wide safeguards for 'high-impact' federal AI come from OMB memo M-25-21 (April 2025): testing before deployment, impact assessments, human oversight and appeals. Because it is executive policy and allows waivers, a future administration can change it without Congress.

choice.p: Supporters of limits on government AI use argue that AI raises the danger of abuse mainly because it...
o: Lets agencies watch and act against many people without needing many cooperating staff
Lets foreign governments run cheap influence campaigns aimed at U.S. voters
Makes federal agency computer systems easier for foreign hackers to break into and disrupt
Lets private companies collect far more data about citizens than agencies can
ow: That is a foreign influence problem; these limits target the government's own coercive powers.
That is a cybersecurity problem; these limits are about what agencies themselves do with AI.
Private data collection is a privacy issue; these limits target government uses like policing and immigration enforcement.

items.p: Why do some antimonopoly scholars want competition policy applied to frontier AI?
items.answer: A few firms could control chips, cloud and frontier models together. That economic power turns into political power (lobbying, influence over information), and concentration creates single points of failure that threaten national security. More independent firms would spread control and add resilience.
keys: a few firms control the AI stack (chips, cloud, models)
economic power becomes political power
concentration creates fragile single points of failure
competition spreads control
items.x: Tejas Narechania and Ganesh Sitaraman make this case in a 2024 Yale Law & Policy Review article, arguing an 'AI oligopoly' raises economic, national security, social and political concerns. Its toolkit includes structural separation, nondiscrimination rules, interoperability and a public option for cloud.

choice.p: What failure do antimonopoly proposals for frontier AI mainly target?
o: A few firms controlling chips, cloud and models, and gaining political power
Many small labs building dangerous models faster than regulators can find and track them
Foreign governments buying large stakes in U.S. AI labs and quietly steering their work
AI companies training their models on creators' work without asking or paying for it
ow: That is a worry about too many developers; antimonopoly proposals worry about too few.
Foreign investment in U.S. firms is screened through national security review, a different tool.
That is a copyright and compensation issue.

items.p: According to supporters, why should programs like the National AI Research Resource (NAIRR) give researchers government-backed computing power and data?
items.answer: Frontier-scale compute is affordable for only a few companies, so research agendas, safety research and the ability to check industry claims depend on them. Public compute lets academic and public-interest researchers study and evaluate AI systems independently.
keys: compute is too expensive for most outside researchers
research and evaluation otherwise depend on a few firms
independent study and checking of industry claims
items.x: NSF launched the NAIRR pilot in January 2024 with partner agencies and more than 25 non-government contributors. The CREATE AI Act (S. 4441, introduced April 29, 2026, by Sens. Young, Heinrich, Rounds and Booker) would make it permanent; as of October 2026 it had only been referred to committee.

choice.p: What do supporters say public compute programs like NAIRR are mainly for?
o: Letting researchers outside big firms study and test AI independently
Giving the military its own frontier models trained on classified data
Guaranteeing chipmakers a buyer for advanced chips they can't export
Keeping advanced chips in government hands so they can't be smuggled abroad
ow: NAIRR serves researchers and educators; military AI is bought through defense procurement.
Public compute buys or borrows capacity for research; it isn't designed as a chip-industry program.
Smuggling is addressed by export controls and chip tracking, a different tool.

items.p: Supporters of federal preemption of state AI laws say it would fix what problem?
items.answer: A patchwork of differing state rules on AI development. Because frontier models are sold nationwide, one state's rules (such as California's) end up governing the whole country, including people with no say, and states lack the capacity and security information to weigh national risks.
keys: a patchwork of conflicting state rules
one state's rules end up governing the whole country
states lack capacity or national security information
one national standard instead
items.x: Ball and Rozenshtein (Lawfare, June 2024) wanted Congress to preempt state rules on how models are developed while leaving most rules on how AI is used to the states. They said they do not necessarily oppose development rules at the federal level.

choice.p: Supporters of federal preemption of state AI laws say it mainly fixes which problem?
o: A patchwork of state rules, letting one state set AI policy for everyone
Too few states regulating AI, leaving most residents without any protections from AI harms
Federal agencies lacking any legal authority to oversee AI companies or their models
States taxing AI data centers so heavily that projects move abroad
ow: That is closer to opponents' worry: preemption without federal rules could leave people unprotected.
Federal agencies already have some authority; preemption is about displacing state law.
Data center taxes are a separate fight; preemption debates center on state rules for AI models and uses.

items.p: Why do many advocates focused on catastrophic AI risk argue that limits on frontier AI eventually need a U.S.-China agreement?
items.answer: Unilateral restraint fails if rivals keep racing, since a country that holds back just cedes ground. Limits above some capability level only work if the leading AI powers accept them together, with verification so that cheating can be detected.
keys: unilateral restraint fails if rivals keep racing
the leading AI powers must accept limits together
verification to detect cheating
items.x: MIRI researchers (Scher, Abecassis, Barnett and Abeyta, 2025) proposed an agreement for a U.S.- and China-led coalition that would cap training compute and prohibit research that advances toward superintelligence, verified by tracking AI chips. They concede the political will for it does not yet exist.

choice.p: Why do many catastrophic-risk advocates argue frontier AI limits eventually need a U.S.-China agreement?
o: One country's restraint is wasted if rivals keep racing, so both must accept limits
International law already bans dangerous AI, so a treaty is needed only to enforce that ban
Chinese labs lead on safety research, so the U.S. needs a treaty to gain access to it
A treaty would let the U.S. lift its chip export controls and sell to China again
ow: No existing treaty bans dangerous AI development; that is why agreements are proposed.
The case for agreements rests on racing dynamics; access to research is a separate issue.
Treaty proposals generally rely on tracking chips; lifting export controls is not their aim.

units.title: Theory of change: risks and assumptions
units.desc: Back to the risks from the first unit: which levers answer which scenario, and what has to be true for a lever’s theory of change to hold.

items.p: Suppose an AI model could give real step-by-step help to someone trying to build a biological weapon. Name two policy tools aimed at reducing that risk.
items.answer: Examples: mandatory screening of DNA synthesis orders and customers; government testing of models for bio capabilities before release; limits on openly releasing model weights above a dangerous-capability threshold; managed access to biological design tools.
keys: DNA synthesis screening
Pre-release dangerous-capability testing
Limits on open-weight release above a threshold
Restricted or managed access to bio design tools
items.x: The tools work at different points. Testing and access limits act on the model; DNA screening acts on the physical step of turning a design into a pathogen, so supporters argue it works whichever model produced the design, as long as screening keeps pace with AI design tools.

choice.p: Which of these is a policy tool proposed to reduce the risk of AI helping someone build a biological weapon?
o: Mandatory screening of DNA synthesis orders
Antitrust review of investments between labs and cloud providers
Logging officials' use of AI chatbots as public records
A temporary pause on permits for new data centers
ow: This targets concentration of market power in AI.
This targets hidden use of AI by government officials.
Local and state data center pauses are mostly about electricity, water and land use.

items.p: Suppose a rival government or criminal group steals the weights of a frontier model, which lets them strip its safeguards and run it freely. Name two policy tools meant to prevent or limit this.
items.answer: Examples: required security standards for model weights and labs, up to defending against nation-state attackers; security conditions on frontier data centers (tied to permits, grid access or contracts); controls on insiders' access to weights; mandatory reporting of weight theft or tampering.
keys: Model weight security standards
Data center security requirements
Insider access controls
Reporting weight theft
items.x: Whoever holds stolen weights can remove the safeguards the developer built and spread the model, and the theft speeds up rivals in a race. Supporters say this makes security the foundation that deployment limits, export controls and pauses depend on.

choice.p: Which of these is a policy tool proposed to prevent theft of a frontier model's weights?
o: Required security levels for model weights, up to nation-state attackers
Mandatory liability insurance sized to the harms a model could cause
An ID for each AI agent, tied to whoever built and runs it
Statutory limits on AI's role in decisions to launch nuclear weapons
ow: Insurance helps pay for harms after they happen; it doesn't secure the weights.
Agent IDs make misbehaving agents traceable; they don't protect stored weights.
This keeps humans in charge of nuclear launch decisions.

items.p: Suppose a model under development starts deceiving its developers and trying to evade their controls. Name two policy tools aimed at catching or containing this.
items.answer: Examples: required reporting of incidents such as loss of control or deceptive behavior; oversight of models labs use internally before release; testing for control-related capabilities; a required, tested ability to shut systems down; government emergency authority to halt a dangerous model; pauses triggered when capability thresholds are crossed.
keys: Incident reporting of deception or loss of control
Oversight of internal deployment
Shutdown capability
Emergency halt authority
Capability-triggered pauses
items.x: Internal use matters here: labs can use their most capable models inside the company, increasingly to do AI research, before anyone outside sees them. Rules that trigger only on public release miss that window.

choice.p: Which of these is a policy tool proposed to catch or contain a model that deceives its developers or evades their controls?
o: A required, tested ability to shut the model down
Know-your-customer checks on cloud computing customers
Mandatory screening of DNA synthesis orders
Multi-vendor rules for government AI purchases
ow: Cloud KYC tracks who rents compute; it doesn't detect a deceptive model.
DNA screening targets bioweapon misuse by people.
Multi-vendor buying targets government dependence on a few firms.

items.p: Suppose a lab uses an unreleased model inside the company for months to write code and run experiments for its next model. Most rules apply only when a model is released to the public. Name two policy tools proposed to bring this internal use under oversight.
items.answer: Examples: confidential reports to a regulator on the risks of internal use; applying the lab's safety framework and access rules to internal models; an internal deployment oversight board; embedded auditors who can see internal systems; government power to restrict or suspend internal use.
keys: Internal-use risk reports to a regulator
Safety frameworks and access rules cover internal models
Internal oversight board
Embedded auditors
Government power to restrict or suspend internal use
items.x: California's SB 53 already requires large developers to send the state quarterly summaries of their internal-use risk assessments, and New York's RAISE Act adds this from 2027. Supporters name two failures it targets: a misaligned model doing AI research could sabotage safety work unseen, and whoever controls the best internal model could use it for private advantage.

choice.p: Which of these is a policy tool proposed to oversee models that labs use internally before public release?
o: Confidential reports to a regulator on internal-use risks
Labels telling the public when they are talking to an AI system
Export licenses for chipmaking equipment sold abroad
Antitrust review of partnerships between labs and cloud providers
ow: AI-interaction labels apply when the public meets a deployed system.
Equipment export licenses govern who can make advanced chips abroad.
This targets concentration of market power in AI.

items.p: Advanced AI could let a small group run large parts of a government or military with few people involved, removing the check that people can refuse illegal orders. Name two policy tools aimed at that risk.
items.answer: Examples: requiring AI used by government to refuse clearly unlawful orders; statutory limits on military and coercive government uses of AI; logging and preserving how officials use AI so it can be reviewed; designing government AI so no single person or small group controls it; audits for hidden loyalties in models.
keys: AI that refuses unlawful orders
Statutory limits on military or government AI
Records of officials' AI use
Distributed control of government AI
Audits for hidden loyalties
items.x: This family of tools tries to keep a 'many hands' check alive once AI can replace the soldiers, analysts and civil servants who might otherwise refuse.

choice.p: Which of these is a policy tool proposed to keep a check in place when AI replaces the people who could refuse illegal orders?
o: Requiring government AI to refuse clearly unlawful orders
Mandatory screening of DNA synthesis orders
Know-your-customer rules for companies that rent out cloud computing
Liability insurance requirements for all frontier AI developers
ow: DNA screening targets bioweapon misuse.
Cloud KYC controls who can rent compute, mainly to enforce export controls.
Insurance helps pay for harms developers' models cause.

items.p: Suppose the US and China are both racing to build more capable AI, and each believes slowing down alone would hand the other a lead. Name two policy tools proposed to reduce the danger of this race.
items.answer: Examples: a US-China dialogue and an AI incident channel; agreed international red lines, such as no AI control of nuclear launches; a treaty capping training compute, verified by chip tracking; funding verification research now; chip export controls, which supporters say keep a US lead that buys time or leverage for a deal.
keys: Dialogue and incident channel
International red lines
Verified treaty capping compute
Verification research or on-chip verification
Export controls to keep a lead (supporters' view)
items.x: Supporters of agreements argue that one country holding back fails if the other keeps racing, so limits above some capability level need both. After a September 2026 summit, the White House said the two countries had agreed to a 'Super Intelligence Dialogue' on AI risks and benefits and a channel for AI incidents; it gave few details on how the channel would work.

choice.p: Which of these is a policy tool proposed to reduce the danger of a US-China AI race?
o: A verified treaty capping training compute
Logging officials' AI chats as federal records
A private right to sue for AI lab whistleblowers
Nondiscrimination rules for AI firms' access to cloud computing
ow: This targets hidden use of AI inside government.
This strengthens protection for lab employees who report dangers.
This targets concentration in cloud markets.

items.p: Competitive pressure can push AI labs to cut safety corners to ship first. Name two policy tools aimed at that dynamic.
items.answer: Examples: a legal duty of care backed by lawsuits; published safety frameworks that labs must follow; independent audits; whistleblower protections for employees; an antitrust safe harbor letting labs coordinate on safety; binding rules that apply to every lab at once.
keys: Duty of care or liability
Required safety frameworks
Independent audits
Whistleblower protections
Antitrust safe harbor for coordination
items.x: Most of these work on incentives: they make skipped precautions costly or visible, or they let labs slow down together without any one of them falling behind.

choice.p: Which of these is a policy tool proposed to stop labs from cutting safety corners to ship first?
o: An antitrust safe harbor so rival labs can agree to slow down together
Identity checks by cloud providers on customers renting AI chips
Logging officials' AI use and keeping the logs as public records
Merger review of investments between frontier labs and cloud providers
ow: Cloud identity checks target export-control gaps, not competition between labs.
AI-use records target misuse inside government.
Merger review targets market concentration; it doesn't change the pressure to ship first.

items.p: Supporters say chip export controls slow rival countries’ frontier AI. Which assumption does that theory of change depend on most?
o: Compute is a binding limit on progress, and controls can’t easily be evaded
Rival countries will agree to match US limits on their own chips
Labs in the US will slow their own progress to match
Models trained abroad can’t be used inside the United States
ow: Export controls work without the target’s agreement; that’s what makes them unilateral.
Export controls restrict sales abroad and don’t ask US labs to slow down.
Where models are used is a separate question.
keys: Compute is a binding constraint
Smuggling, cloud rental or domestic chips can’t easily replace it
items.x: Each way around the controls is a crack in the theory: smuggling, renting chips from cloud data centers abroad, and building domestic chips. That is why supporters pair export controls with location verification, cloud rules and controls on chipmaking equipment.

items.p: A conditional pause stops work when a model crosses a dangerous capability threshold. What must hold for this to prevent harm?
o: Evaluations must detect the capability before the model is deployed or stolen
Every country must already have a law banning superintelligence
Labs must publish their model weights so anyone can test them
Data center construction must already be paused
ow: A pause can be adopted by one country or by labs; a ban is a different lever.
Published weights can't be recalled, so a pause could no longer contain a dangerous model.
A conditional pause works whatever the stock of data centers.
keys: Dangerous capabilities are detected in time
Before deployment or theft
items.x: A pause triggered by a missed capability does nothing. Researchers also worry that models may hide capabilities during testing (sometimes called sandbagging), which would break the trigger.

items.p: Supporters of a national AI data center moratorium say it would slow frontier AI. Which assumption does that depend on?
o: New data centers are the binding limit on progress, and building can’t simply move abroad
Existing data centers will be shut down during the moratorium
AI labs will lobby Congress to end the moratorium quickly
Electricity prices will fall once construction stops
ow: Moratorium proposals stop new building and upgrades; existing centers keep running.
That might happen, but it isn’t what the slowing argument rests on.
Prices are a separate motive for local moratoria.
keys: New capacity is the binding constraint
Building can’t just move to other countries
items.x: One national moratorium bill would also bar exports of AI computing hardware to countries without comparable safeguards, an attempt to close the move-abroad gap.

items.p: Liability levers reduce risk by making labs expect to pay for harms. Name two conditions that must hold for liability to deter catastrophic risk.
items.answer: The lab must be able to pay (a true catastrophe could exceed any firm’s assets); victims must be able to sue and show the lab caused the harm; and the lab must believe it will still exist and be held responsible after the harm.
keys: The lab can pay for the harm
Victims can sue and prove causation
The lab expects to be held responsible afterward
items.x: Gabriel Weil, a liability scholar, notes that a true catastrophe would exceed what any firm could pay, which is why some propose insurance mandates or punitive damages for smaller, warning-shot harms. Causation is hard when a model is one of many contributors to a harm.

choice.p: Why do some liability scholars think ordinary lawsuits may not deter the worst AI catastrophes?
o: The harm could exceed anything a lab could pay, so the threat of paying stops scaling
Courts are forbidden from hearing cases about software
Labs are already fully insured against every possible harm
Lawsuits can only be brought by the federal government
ow: Courts hear software cases; there is debate over whether software counts as a product.
Several large insurers have instead sought permission to exclude AI risks from their policies.
Private parties can sue under negligence and product liability.

items.p: A kill switch mandate makes a lab keep a tested way to shut down its models. When would the switch fail to help?
o: When harm isn’t noticed in time, or the model has copied itself beyond the lab’s control
When the model is offered to customers through the lab's own servers
When the government hasn’t also passed a duty of care
When the lab publishes a transparency report on the model
ow: Hosted access is where a switch works best, since the lab controls the servers.
A switch works without a liability rule.
Reporting and a switch don’t interfere with each other.
keys: Harm must be noticed in time
The model must still be within the lab’s reach
items.x: Some proposals add an independent group that keeps testing the switch, because a capability that has never been used may not work when it is needed.

units.title: Pros and cons
units.desc: Objections that recur across many levers, then the main objections to each family, then how levers depend on each other.

items.p: Some objections come up against many different levers. Match each objection to what it means.
pairs: Fast-moving technology makes fixed rules out of date
Large incumbents shape the rules in their own favor
Box-ticking compliance gives a false sense of safety
Activity moves around the rule or to other countries
Regulators lack the expertise or access to check compliance
items.x: Recognizing the recurring objection makes it easier to see when a design answers it: sunset clauses for pacing, independence rules for capture, outside verification for safety-washing, international agreements for offshoring.

items.p: Critics of compute thresholds, such as 10^26 operations, often say they are a weak way to decide which models a rule covers. Why?
o: Compute is only a rough stand-in for dangerous capability, and efficiency gains move the line
Labs don’t keep any records of how much compute they use
Thresholds are illegal under the Constitution’s commerce clause
Only chips made in the US can be counted toward a threshold
ow: Large labs track compute closely; the problem is what the number stands for.
No court has held compute thresholds unconstitutional.
Thresholds count training operations wherever the chips were made.
keys: Compute is a proxy for capability
Algorithmic efficiency makes thresholds go stale
items.x: ControlAI, a UK advocacy group, argues thresholds are easy to game and catch harmless work such as video generation. Supporters reply that compute is the only measure available before a model exists, so thresholds work best as a trigger for closer looks.

items.p: Some laws require large developers to get an annual independent audit of whether they follow their own published safety framework. What important question does this kind of audit leave unanswered?
items.answer: Whether the lab's own framework is good enough. A compliance audit checks that the lab does what its framework says, so a weak framework that the lab faithfully follows can pass with a clean audit.
keys: whether the framework itself is adequate or strong enough
a weak framework that is faithfully followed can pass
items.x: Illinois's audits begin January 1, 2028. The auditor can't have a financial stake in the developer, pay can't depend on the results, and a redacted report is published and sent to a state agency and the attorney general. The federal FRONTIER Act bill goes further for the very largest developers: a licensed verifier would judge whether their framework and safeguards achieve "acceptable levels of catastrophic risk mitigation."

choice.p: What does a framework compliance audit, like the one Illinois SB 315 requires, leave unchecked?
o: Whether the lab's safety framework is adequate for its risks
Whether the lab is actually following the safety framework it published
Whether the auditor has a financial stake in the lab it is auditing
Whether a summary of the audit findings is published for the public
ow: That is exactly what a compliance audit checks.
Illinois bars auditors with a financial interest in the developer, so independence is covered.
Illinois requires the developer to publish a high-level summary and a redacted copy of the report.

items.p: Some laws require large AI developers to publish a safety framework they write themselves, and to follow it. Name two objections or weaknesses critics raise.
items.answer: Examples: labs pick their own rules, so a vague framework is hard to violate (the Midas Project); published frameworks score poorly on risk-management criteria (SaferAI); labs can rewrite frameworks and have weakened pledges to pause (Future of Life Institute); state rules could slow US innovation in the race with China (industry groups, Trump administration).
keys: labs choose their own rules, so vague frameworks are hard to violate
existing frameworks are weak or underspecified
labs can rewrite or weaken their frameworks
burden on innovation or conflict with the federal AI agenda
items.x: Tyler Johnston of the Midas Project, which alleged in September 2026 that OpenAI broke SB 53, said "it's totally up to them to choose what the rules are." OpenAI said it was confident it complied. A SaferAI study scored 12 companies' frameworks against 65 criteria and found a median score of 18%.

choice.p: Which of these is an objection critics raise to laws requiring labs to publish and follow a safety framework they write themselves?
o: Labs pick their own rules, so a vague framework is hard to break
The law imposes one government safety standard that fits no lab well
Published frameworks expose trade secrets because nothing can be redacted
The law lets anyone harmed by AI sue the developer for unlimited damages
ow: Each lab defines its own thresholds, which is why critics worry about vagueness.
SB 53 lets developers redact trade secrets and security details if they explain each redaction.
Only the attorney general enforces SB 53, with penalties capped at $1 million per violation.

items.p: A country imposes strict limits on frontier AI that no other country matches. What objection do critics commonly raise?
o: Development moves to countries without the limits, so global risk may not fall
Domestic labs will be forced to publish their model weights
Courts will be unable to hear any AI liability cases
The limits will automatically expire after one year
ow: Limits don’t force publication of weights.
Domestic limits don’t affect courts’ jurisdiction.
Limits expire only if written with a sunset.
keys: Activity moves abroad
Rivals gain ground while global risk stays
items.x: This is the main argument for pairing domestic limits with export controls or international agreements. Supporters of unilateral rules reply that a few countries host nearly all frontier development, so domestic rules reach most of it.

items.p: Mandatory incident reporting: developers must tell a government agency about serious AI safety incidents within a set number of hours or days. Name two objections or weaknesses critics raise.
items.answer: Examples: definitions that require actual harm or exclude testing can miss serious near misses (Arnold and Llerena, LawAI); vague terms such as 'critical safety incident' leave firms unsure how to comply (NetChoice); a patchwork of unstandardized reporting yields data that can't be compared (CSET); reports help only if the agency can investigate.
keys: definitions miss near misses or events in testing
vague terms make compliance unclear
unstandardized, fragmented data
the agency may lack capacity to act
items.x: The objections come from both directions: safety researchers say current rules are too narrow, while industry groups say they are too vague or burdensome. Arnold and Llerena urge giving agencies rulemaking and investigative powers. California's SB 53 exempts incident reports from its public records law; from 2027 the state also sends lawmakers and the governor an anonymized annual summary.

choice.p: Which of these is a weakness critics see in current mandatory AI incident reporting rules?
o: Definitions requiring actual harm can miss serious near misses
Incident reports are published right away, which tips off attackers
Reports go to Congress, which lacks technical staff to read them
Any model with a reported incident must be shut down permanently
ow: California exempts incident reports from its public records law, and its annual report to lawmakers is anonymized.
Reports go to an executive agency, such as California's Office of Emergency Services.
Reporting rules require notice; tying reports to shutdown powers is a separate proposal.

items.p: Compute reporting: developers must notify the government of training runs above a compute threshold, such as 10^26 operations. Name two objections critics raise.
