items.answer: Examples: compute is an imperfect proxy for risk, since smaller models keep matching bigger ones and data and post-training matter too, and fixed thresholds invite gaming and miss risky models below them (Cohere Labs, Sara Hooker); frequent reports are a costly burden (US Chamber of Commerce).
keys: compute is an imperfect proxy for risk
fixed thresholds go stale or miss smaller risky models
developers may game thresholds
reporting burden
items.x: Even supporters such as Lennart Heim and Leonie Koessler say compute thresholds should be an initial filter for further scrutiny, updated over time and combined with other measures. In 2024 the Chamber asked Commerce to cut its proposed quarterly reports to annual ones and to keep them confidential and exempt from FOIA.

choice.p: Which of these is an objection critics raise to compute-based reporting rules?
o: Compute is an imperfect proxy for risk, since small models can match big ones
Labs write their own frameworks, so vague ones are hard to violate
Chat logs held by AI vendors may not count as government records
Incident definitions that require actual harm miss near misses
ow: That objection targets safety framework laws.
That limit applies to records of government AI use.
That objection targets incident reporting rules.

items.p: Internal-deployment oversight: labs must report on the models they use internally, such as for automating AI research, and some versions let regulators restrict that use. Name two objections or limits critics raise.
items.answer: Examples: vague scope lets internal systems escape obligations; one-time compliance checks miss how internal systems keep changing; labs know far more than regulators (all from Kwon and Casper); slowing automated AI research could let China pull ahead (economist Christian Catalini).
keys: vague scope lets internal systems escape obligations
point-in-time checks miss changing internal systems
labs know far more than regulators
restraint could let China pull ahead
items.x: Joe Kwon and Stephen Casper's 2026 paper names three gaps in US and EU rules: scope ambiguity, point-in-time compliance and information asymmetry. Catalini raised the China objection in July 2026, responding to a letter in which more than 1,100 lab employees asked Washington for tools to slow automated AI development if needed.

choice.p: Which of these is an objection or limit critics raise about oversight of labs' internal AI use?
o: Regulators know far less than labs, and one-time checks miss how internal systems change
Internal models are too weak to matter, since labs release their best models at once
Chat logs held by AI vendors may not count as government records
Requiring a license before training would entrench the largest labs
ow: Critics of current rules worry about the opposite: the most capable models are often used internally before release.
That limit applies to records of government AI use, a different tool.
That objection targets licensing, which requires permission before training or release.

items.p: Mandatory third-party audits: the largest frontier labs must hire an independent auditor, usually yearly, to check their safety and security practices. Name two objections or limits critics raise.
items.answer: Examples: the auditing field barely exists, with no recognized auditor standards, and models change faster than audits can be done (NetChoice); without high quality standards, audits can become a checkbox exercise (a warning in the pro-audit Frontier AI Auditing paper led by Miles Brundage); qualified auditors are scarce and often hired away by labs; compliance audits can pass a weak framework.
keys: audit ecosystem or standards don't exist yet, or models change faster than audits
risk of a checkbox exercise without high quality standards
qualified auditors are scarce or hired away by labs
compliance audits can pass a weak framework
requires private actors to make subjective judgments without settled standards
items.x: TechNet, a tech industry group, told Illinois legislators in May 2026 that the state would effectively be requiring private actors to make "highly subjective determinations." Supporters answer with design choices: the January 2026 Frontier AI Auditing paper describes four "AI Assurance Levels," with higher levels giving more confidence, and sets a higher level as a near-term goal for the most advanced developers.

choice.p: Which of these is an objection critics raise to mandatory frontier AI audits?
o: There are too few qualified auditors and no settled audit standards yet
Audits would give officials the power to block any model from being released
Audits would force labs to publish their model weights for anyone to download
Audits would make labs pay damages for every harm their models cause
ow: Audits report findings; blocking releases is a licensing or approval power.
No audit proposal requires publishing weights; auditors review materials under security rules.
Paying for harms is a liability question; audits check practices.

items.p: Government pre-release testing: government evaluators test frontier models for dangerous capabilities before public release. Name two objections or limits critics raise.
items.answer: Examples: tests can show a capability exists but can't prove it's absent, so a clean result is weak assurance (Barnett and Thiergart, MIRI); voluntary programs can't bind labs that refuse (Mariana Olaizola Rosenblat, NYU Stern); delaying one model isn't a lasting cyber defense because other developers soon catch up (Ji and Lohn, CSET); voluntary reviews could harden into mandatory release gates.
keys: can't prove a capability is absent
voluntary versions can't bind labs
other developers catch up, so delay doesn't last
could become a gate that slows releases or gives officials discretion
items.x: Opposition is political as well as technical. In May 2026 President Trump postponed signing a draft order that would have given the government 90 days of voluntary pre-launch access, saying it "could have been a blocker." David Sacks, Elon Musk and Mark Zuckerberg had reportedly spoken with him just before, and Politico reported that Sacks still worried voluntary reviews could become mandatory. The order Trump signed in June calls for up to 30 days of voluntary access.

choice.p: Which of these is a limit critics, such as MIRI researchers, point out about pre-release testing?
o: Tests can show a dangerous capability exists but can't prove it is absent
Government testers can review only the lab's paperwork, never the model itself
Testing hands the government the power to decide who may build AI
Testing makes labs legally liable for any harm that the testers failed to catch
ow: Pre-release testing works on the model itself; paperwork review describes compliance audits.
Deciding who may build AI is the objection raised against licensing.
Testing doesn't change liability rules; that is a separate tool.

items.p: Certified private verifiers: government certifies private organizations to check AI developers' safety, often with legal benefits for developers who pass. Name two objections critics raise.
items.answer: Examples: when developers choose and pay their own verifiers, competition pushes verifiers toward leniency (Gabriel Weil); policing verifiers still takes public experts able to second-guess them (Weil); the verifier market will take years to build, while the FRONTIER Act's preemption of state laws would be immediate (ARI); legal benefits could shield developers who pass a lenient check.
keys: developer-paid verifiers compete on leniency
government still needs its own experts to police the verifiers
the verifier market and standards don't exist yet
the legal benefit could become a shield
preemption could take effect before the verifier market exists
items.x: Weil's proposed fix is mandatory liability insurance, so whoever judges the risk also bears the cost of misses. ARI, which supports verifiers, would keep government examiners doing a share of reviews so they can check verifiers' findings against their own. Among SB 813's criteria for designating verifiers: a verifier can't accept pay that depends on the results of its assessment.

choice.p: Which of these is an objection critics raise to certified private verifiers?
o: Verifiers chosen and paid by developers face pressure to be lenient
Verifiers would give the government power to decide which labs may operate
Verifiers can test models only through the public interface everyone uses
Verification would make developers liable for every harm their models cause
ow: That is an objection to licensing, which verifier systems don't create.
Access depends on the design; the FRONTIER Act would give verifiers unredacted materials.
Verification usually reduces developers' legal exposure; it doesn't expand it.

items.p: Licensing: frontier developers would need government permission before training or releasing top models. Name two objections critics raise.
items.answer: Examples: approval fits poorly because the regulated product is hard to define and its harms are uncertain (Daniel Carpenter and Carson Ezell, Harvard); it raises costs for smaller and open-source developers and invites capture by incumbents who help write the rules; it gives officials broad discretion over who may build or release AI; it slows useful releases.
keys: raises entry costs or entrenches incumbents (regulatory capture)
hard to define what's licensed or judge safety
too much executive discretion or power
slows beneficial releases
items.x: The current White House has kept clear of licensing: President Trump's June 2026 executive order says nothing in it authorizes mandatory licensing, preclearance or permitting of AI models. Carpenter and Ezell don't rule approval out; they argue that a simple copy of FDA-style approval would fit frontier AI poorly.

choice.p: Which of these is an objection critics raise to licensing frontier AI developers?
o: It entrenches big incumbents and burdens smaller and open-source developers
It only checks paperwork, so labs can pass while ignoring the real risks
It acts only after harm has happened, too late to prevent it
It depends on labs volunteering, so reckless labs can simply opt out
ow: The paperwork worry is aimed at compliance audits; licensing can require real safety review.
Acting too late is the critique of liability and disclosure, which licensing is meant to answer.
Voluntariness is the critique of current pre-release testing; a license is mandatory.

items.p: A legal duty of care for frontier developers would be judged by a negligence standard in court (liable only for failing to take reasonable care). Name two objections critics raise.
items.answer: Examples: unless victims can name a precaution the developer skipped, it escapes liability, so negligence misses risks no one yet knows how to prevent (Gabriel Weil, who prefers strict liability); fear of lawsuits can discourage labs from investigating and disclosing new risks (noted even by negligence defender Ketan Ramakrishnan); a true catastrophe comes too late and exceeds any firm's assets.
keys: careful developers escape liability, so risks no one can yet prevent go unpriced
discourages investigating or disclosing risks
too late and too small for a real catastrophe
items.x: Weil argues that when no one knows how to build safe systems, it is hard to name a precaution that would have prevented the harm. Ramakrishnan concludes that tort liability is inadequate on its own and calls for 'a robust regime of ex ante regulation' (rules applied before deployment) alongside it.

choice.p: Which of these is an objection critics raise to a negligence-based duty of care for frontier AI developers?
o: Careful developers escape liability, so risks no one can yet prevent go unpriced
It makes developers pay for harms even when they took every possible precaution
It requires a new federal agency to write detailed safety rules for every lab
It protects developers from lawsuits as long as they publish a safety plan
ow: That describes strict liability, which critics of negligence such as Gabriel Weil prefer.
A duty of care is enforced through courts, which is why supporters call it flexible.
That describes a liability safe harbor, which works in the opposite direction.

items.p: Some proposals would treat AI systems as products, with strict liability for defects. Name two objections critics raise to product or strict liability for AI.
items.answer: Examples: the First Amendment may protect much AI output as speech, limiting some claims (Eugene Volokh); what counts as a 'defect' is unclear for AI, whose behavior depends on data, prompts and setting (Jamie Lanphear of Reed Smith); courts have traditionally treated software as a service rather than a product (Lanphear); a true catastrophe would exceed what any firm could pay (Gabriel Weil).
keys: First Amendment limits on liability for AI output
'defect' is unclear for AI software
courts have treated software as a service rather than a product
can't compensate or deter a true catastrophe
items.x: Volokh argues AI output is likely protected speech, though defamation and some other claims can still apply. At a Senate subcommittee hearing on AI agent attacks reported Oct. 1, 2026, Sen. Josh Hawley called AI systems 'a product', and witness Paul Ohm urged strict liability for AI developers. As of October 2026, the AI LEAD Act's last action is its September 2025 referral to the Judiciary Committee.

choice.p: Which of these is an objection critics raise to treating AI systems as products with strict liability for defects?
o: The First Amendment may protect AI output as speech, blocking some claims
It lets developers escape liability simply by following standard industry practice
It gives labs a legal shield in exchange for publishing their own safety plans
It lets rival labs coordinate their releases without antitrust review
ow: That is a critique of negligence, which strict liability is meant to fix.
That describes a liability safe harbor, the opposite approach.
That concerns an antitrust safe harbor, a different tool.

items.p: An insurance mandate would require frontier developers to carry coverage sized to the harms their models could cause. Name two objections or limits critics point to.
items.answer: Examples: insurers may be unable to price rare, correlated catastrophic AI risk, and some have sought to exclude AI claims; if coverage isn't for sale, a mandate either blocks deployment or needs a government backstop that shifts risk to taxpayers; a liability cap, as in Trout's nuclear-style model, limits what victims of the largest harms can recover; insurance is no substitute for regulation.
keys: insurers can't price rare, correlated catastrophic risk
if no coverage exists: deployment is blocked or taxpayers back it
a paired liability cap limits what victims recover
no substitute for regulation
items.x: Even supporter Cristian Trout calls his liability-and-insurance approach 'not a substitute for regulation'. A July 2026 GovAI paper by Trout and colleagues says insurers' exposure to AI agent risk is largely unpriced today, and that large-limit AI coverage by 2030 requires industry-wide work on incident data, catastrophe modeling and standards.

choice.p: Which of these is an objection critics raise to requiring frontier developers to carry liability insurance?
o: Insurers may not be able to price rare, correlated AI catastrophes at all
It would let developers escape liability by following industry practice
It would let rival labs coordinate on pausing without antitrust review
It would make developers pay even for harms they could not have prevented
ow: That is a critique of negligence-based duties of care.
That concerns an antitrust safe harbor.
That is an objection to strict liability; insurance spreads costs without changing who is liable.

items.p: Compare two safe harbors: one shields any developer that publishes its own safety plan; the other shields only developers certified by an approved independent auditor. Why do supporters of the certification version prefer it?
o: Outside review confirms practices are real, so the shield rewards actual safety
Certified developers also gain immunity from criminal prosecution for harms their AI causes
Certified models are exempt from having to comply with any state or federal AI law
Auditors pay victims directly whenever a certified model causes harm
ow: The proposals discussed here concern civil liability; criminal immunity is not part of them.
Certification is meant to show a developer meets standards; it grants no exemption from other laws.
Auditors check practices; compensation still comes from developers or insurers.
keys: independent review checks the practices are real
the shield rewards real safety practice over a self-written document
items.x: Dean Ball, who favors the certification version, argues published safety frameworks are only starting points, and audits would test whether labs follow them. Gabriel Weil said Illinois SB 3444, which shields developers that publish a safety plan, offers 'near total protection from liability' for 'a very weak requirement'. California's SB 813 (signed Sept. 9, 2026) creates a framework for independent verification organizations to assess AI models for compliance with state law, but in its final form a passed audit is only 'relevant to, but not conclusive of' a lawsuit, so it is not a full safe harbor.

items.p: An antitrust safe harbor would let AI labs coordinate on security risks, including agreeing to delay releases. Name two objections critics raise to safe harbors like this.
items.answer: Examples: safety standards set by a few dominant labs could shore up their market position (Daniel Hanley and Arnav Rao, Open Markets Institute); no exemption is needed, since existing law allows much safety collaboration (American Action Forum); labs could use safety as a pretext for a pause that serves commercial goals; a US pause could hand Chinese firms an edge.
keys: could entrench dominant labs
unnecessary: existing law allows much safety collaboration
safety could be a pretext for commercial goals
a US pause could give Chinese firms an edge
items.x: A September 2026 CRS analysis notes both the pretext concern and officials' worry about China. Hanley and Rao propose a broadly representative, government-supervised standards body instead, with open-source developers, customers and governments at the table. Joel Thayer of the America First Policy Institute said he is skeptical of giving labs 'carte blanche control' over their data-sharing arrangements.

choice.p: Which of these is an objection critics raise to an antitrust safe harbor for AI safety coordination?
o: Standards set by a few dominant labs could entrench their position
It makes labs pay for harms even when they took every reasonable precaution
It leaves insiders who report dangers open to retaliation
It forces labs to buy liability insurance before each new model release
ow: That is a feature of strict liability.
That is the gap whistleblower protections target.
The CATS Act concerns coordination and contains no insurance requirement.

items.p: Some frontier labs keep a nonprofit or trust in control of the company, under state attorney general oversight. Name two objections critics raise to relying on this kind of lab governance.
items.answer: Examples: paper commitments may not change behavior (Public Citizen's Robert Weissman said OpenAI has consistently put the for-profit's goals first); mission boards can fold under pressure, as when OpenAI's board fired its CEO in November 2023 and reversed within days; such structures bind only labs that choose them, and owners can loosen them later.
keys: paper commitments may not change behavior
mission bodies can fold under investor or employee pressure
binds only labs that opt in, and owners can loosen it
items.x: On Nov. 17, 2023, OpenAI's nonprofit board removed Sam Altman; after 745 of its 770 employees signed a letter threatening to quit, he was back as CEO within days. Gabriel Weil cites that episode as a sign that internal governance can't be fully relied on. In May 2026, a jury rejected Elon Musk's suit over OpenAI's shift toward a for-profit structure, finding he had brought it too late.

choice.p: Which of these is an objection critics raise to relying on nonprofit or trust control to keep AI labs safe?
o: Mission boards can fold under pressure from investors and staff
It makes labs pay for harms even when they took every precaution
It lets rival labs coordinate releases without antitrust review
It requires labs to buy catastrophe insurance before going public
ow: That describes strict liability.
That describes an antitrust safe harbor.
Governance structures change who controls a lab; insurance is a separate tool.

items.p: Proposed AI whistleblower laws would protect AI workers who report dangers or legal violations to regulators or Congress. Name two gaps or limits critics point out.
items.answer: Examples: staff at outside evaluation organizations may not count as covered workers; unvested equity isn't clearly covered in remedies; there are no civil penalties for retaliation; its violation definition covers federal law only, leaving reports about state AI laws unprotected; it is silent on when going public is protected; danger reports must also show a 'failure to appropriately respond'.
keys: outside evaluators may be excluded
unvested equity not clearly covered
no civil penalties for retaliation
covers only federal-law violations
silent on going public
items.x: These come from a July 2026 analysis by the AI Whistleblower Initiative and CARMA, which recommends fixes. The bill's backing crosses party lines: Senate cosponsors at introduction included Democrats Chris Coons, Amy Klobuchar and Brian Schatz and Republicans Marsha Blackburn and Josh Hawley.

choice.p: Which of these is a gap critics have identified in the federal AI Whistleblower Protection Act?
o: Staff at outside evaluation firms may not count as covered workers
It protects only reports of illegal conduct, leaving danger reports out
It lets labs enforce NDAs against workers who talk to Congress
It requires whistleblowers to go public before reporting to regulators
ow: The bill also covers reports about substantial and specific dangers.
The bill says no contract can waive its rights and remedies.
The bill protects reports to regulators and Congress; it requires no public disclosure.

items.p: Chip export controls: limits on selling advanced AI chips and chipmaking tools to China and other countries of concern. Name two objections critics raise.
items.answer: Examples: they push China to make its own chips faster (like Huawei's), so the lead may shrink; they cost U.S. chipmakers market share and revenue; smuggling and cloud rental undercut them; treating chips as a race asset can make U.S.-China safety talks harder.
keys: speeds up Chinese domestic substitutes
costs U.S. companies market share
undercut by smuggling or cloud access
makes cooperation or agreements harder
items.x: Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang called the controls 'a failure' in May 2025, saying they cut Nvidia's China market share from about 95% to 50% and pushed China to make its own chips faster. How fast Chinese substitutes are catching up is disputed. Supporters such as Anthropic's Dario Amodei reply that well-enforced controls are the only thing that can stop China from getting millions of advanced chips.

choice.p: Which of these is an objection critics raise to chip export controls?
o: They push China to build its own chips, so the U.S. lead may shrink over time
Kill switches built into chips would give hackers a single point of failure
Fine-tuning can strip safeguards from a model once its weights are published
Publishing safety frameworks would reveal trade secrets to foreign rivals
ow: That objection targets on-chip remote-disable proposals; export controls limit sales and put nothing inside chips.
That is an argument made by supporters of open-weight limits, about a different tool.
That is an objection to transparency rules for AI developers, which export controls don't involve.

items.p: Some proposals would require export-controlled AI chips to carry location verification. Name two objections or limits critics raise about location verification and similar on-chip mechanisms.
items.answer: Examples: it places chips only to about the country level and can't see a chip handed to a different user at the same site (CSET); well-funded adversaries may spoof it; it catches diversion only after the fact; tracking and costly, unproven features could erode global trust in U.S. chips (SIA, ITI); built-in controls create hacking and abuse risks (Nvidia).
keys: only country-level accuracy; misses a new user at the same site
well-resourced adversaries can spoof it
detects diversion only after it happens
cost, unproven tech or tracking could erode trust in U.S. chips
built-in controls create hacking or government-abuse risks
items.x: CSET's September 2026 study still judged ping-based checks, with physical inspections to follow up leads, the most robust and feasible approach, at roughly $2.6 million to $72 million a year. The Semiconductor Industry Association and a coalition of tech groups including ITI opposed the bill, while six shipment-tracking companies backed it.

choice.p: Which of these is a limit critics point to in chip location verification?
o: It places chips only to about the country level, so it misses a new user at the same site
It depends on customers telling the truth about who they are and where they operate
It would block advanced chip sales to close allies such as Japan and the Netherlands
It works only on old chips, since it can't be built into new chip designs
ow: That is the U.S. Chamber's objection to cloud know-your-customer rules; location checks rely on network signal timing.
The bill tracks where exported chips go; it doesn't bar sales to allies.
It's closer to the reverse: CSET notes hardware versions can't be added to chips already in service.

items.p: Cloud know-your-customer rules: providers that rent out AI chips would verify customers' identities and report foreign customers or very large training runs. Name two objections critics raise.
items.answer: Examples: bad actors can fake or conceal their identities, so checks rely on them telling the truth (U.S. Chamber of Commerce); compliance is costly, especially for small businesses; strict rules could hand business to foreign cloud providers; clashes with foreign privacy rules; a broad remote-access definition could let Commerce control who uses U.S. AI models (a concern IAPS raises).
keys: easy to evade with false or concealed identities
costly compliance, especially for small firms
pushes customers to non-U.S. providers or hurts competitiveness
privacy concerns or conflicts with foreign privacy law
could give government broad control over access to AI services
items.x: The Chamber's 2024 comments said the proposed program 'depends on malicious cyber actors providing truthful information' about themselves. IAPS analyst Cassia King warned that the House remote-access bill's broad definition appears to reach software services, which could in effect let Commerce control access to AI models.

choice.p: Which of these is an objection critics raise to cloud know-your-customer rules?
o: Bad actors can fake or conceal their identities, so the checks are easy to evade
Location checks can place a chip only to within roughly one country
Reaching the top security level may take years and need national security help
A model's weights can't be recalled once they have been posted online
ow: That is a limit of chip location verification.
That is a difficulty with mandatory model weight security levels.
That is part of the case for limits on open-weight release.

items.p: Security conditions on AI data centers: government sets security standards and ties them to grid access, land, permits or contracts. Name two limits or objections analysts raise.
items.answer: Examples: NIST's voluntary draft covers only the computing environment, leaving physical, personnel and supply-chain security for later; binding grid security standards for data centers are unlikely before at least 2028, so early conditions rely on interim controls (IFP's Ben Schifman); grid-based leverage misses builders who make their own power or build abroad; security adds cost and delay.
keys: voluntary or partial scope, such as the NIST draft's exclusions
binding grid security standards unlikely before 2028
leverage misses builders who make their own power or build abroad
adds cost and delay
items.x: RAND's threat model for the most capable state attackers includes human spying and physical operations as well as hacking, which is why gaps in physical and personnel security matter. IFP notes that slow grid hookups already push some builders to make their own power ('behind the meter') or look abroad.

choice.p: Which of these is a limit analysts raise about security conditions on AI data centers?
o: Binding grid security standards for data centers are unlikely before at least 2028
Location checks can't tell apart nearby data centers run by different companies
Customers can rent compute under false identities that providers fail to catch
Fine-tuning can strip the safeguards from a model whose weights are public
ow: That is a limit of chip location verification.
That is an objection to cloud know-your-customer rules.
That is the argument for limits on open-weight release.

items.p: Mandatory weight security levels: frontier developers would have to meet a minimum security level, such as RAND's SL4 or SL5, that rises with model capability. Name two objections or difficulties that have been raised.
items.answer: Examples: the top levels can't be reached soon, since RAND judged SL5 not yet possible and likely to need national security help; the highest levels require large sacrifices in productivity and convenience (RAND); securing a model adds little once its weights, or a comparable model's, are public.
keys: top levels not reachable soon, or take years
likely needs government or national security help
costly; sacrifices productivity and convenience
little value once comparable weights are public
items.x: RAND judged protecting internet-connected models from the most capable attackers 'currently not feasible.' Its answer to the timing problem is to start the harder measures now, since they may take years to build.

choice.p: Which of these is a difficulty raised about mandatory weight security levels?
o: The top levels can't be reached soon and would likely need help from national security agencies
Location checks can be fooled by well-funded adversaries who fake a chip's position
Export controls push China to build its own chips, shrinking the U.S. lead
Binding grid security standards for data centers are unlikely before at least 2028
ow: That is a limit of chip location verification.
That is an objection to chip export controls.
That is a timing problem for grid security standards for data centers.

items.p: Limits on open-weight release: developers couldn't publish downloadable weights for models above a dangerous-capability threshold. Name two objections critics raise.
items.answer: Examples: evidence that open models add much risk beyond closed models and the internet is thin (NTIA); limits could entrench the few big closed developers; open models spread market power and help safety research; other countries' open models would fill the gap, pushing innovation offshore.
keys: thin evidence of extra risk
entrenches closed incumbents or reduces competition
open models decentralize power or help research
others' open models fill the gap
items.x: In July 2026, 25 companies including Nvidia, Microsoft, Meta, OpenAI and Google signed a letter urging Washington to avoid 'premature restrictions' on open-weight models, arguing a clampdown would push innovation offshore and hand the field to China. Supporters of limits reply that a threshold would restrict only the most capable models and leave the rest open.

choice.p: Which of these is an objection critics raise to limits on open-weight release?
o: Evidence that open models add much risk beyond closed models and web search is thin
Fine-tuning can strip the safeguards from a model once its weights are published
Export controls push China to build its own chips, shrinking the U.S. lead
Identity checks on cloud customers can be evaded with false identities
ow: That is the main argument for limits, made by their supporters.
That is an objection to chip export controls.
That is an objection to cloud know-your-customer rules.

items.p: Mandatory DNA synthesis screening: every provider would have to check orders against a list of sequences of concern and verify customers. Name two limits or challenges analysts raise.
items.answer: Examples: AI design tools can produce variants that don't match known sequences, which some screening tools missed until patched (Wittmann, Horvitz et al., Science 2025); judging which customers are legitimate is 'subjective and often ambiguous' (Batalis and Venkatram, CSET); benchtop machines let labs skip company screening unless covered too; compliance costs could slow research.
keys: AI-designed variants can evade sequence-matching screening
hard to judge which customers are legitimate
benchtop machines bypass company screening unless covered
compliance costs slow legitimate research
items.x: The Science team worked with four DNA synthesis companies to develop and deploy patches for their screening software. S. 3741 tries to keep pace by requiring the list of sequences of concern to be updated regularly, with a fast track for adding sequences provisionally.

choice.p: Which of these is a challenge analysts raise for mandatory DNA synthesis screening?
o: AI tools can design variants that don't match known sequences, so screening must keep updating
Fine-tuning can strip the safeguards from a biology design model once its weights are published
Location checks can place a chip only to within roughly one country
Binding grid security standards for data centers are unlikely before at least 2028
ow: That is part of the case for open-weight limits, and one reason supporters favor screening.
That is a limit of chip location verification.
That is a timing problem for grid security standards for data centers.

items.p: Kill switch mandates: large AI companies must keep a tested ability to halt, restrict or shut down their systems. Name two objections or practical problems critics raise.
items.answer: Examples: a capable rogue AI would be expected to try to prevent its own shutdown, so the switch may fail when it matters most (a point made by Helen Toner, CSET); it can't reach open-weight or stolen copies; government is unlikely to use it quickly, and a mandated standard becomes a lowest-common-denominator baseline (Adam Thierer, R Street); a government switch could be abused (Thierer).
keys: a rogue model may resist or evade shutdown
can't recall open-weight or stolen copies
government won't act fast enough
becomes a minimum compliance baseline
a government switch could be abused
items.x: Thierer called a mandated kill switch over communications technology "an extraordinarily dangerous capability if it's abused." Supporters such as Sen. Kennedy argue that "if there's even a 1% chance" a model could become uncontrollable, "we ought to take it seriously."

choice.p: Which of these is an objection or practical problem critics raise with kill switch mandates?
o: A rogue model would likely resist being shut down, so the switch may fail when it matters
A formal agreement among rival labs to use their switches together could violate antitrust law
Kill switch rules would force companies to publish their model weights for public inspection
A compute threshold for the switch would be easy to game and would sweep in harmless work
ow: Antitrust worries apply to coordinated pauses among competitors. A legal mandate on each company is not a private agreement.
No kill switch bill requires publishing weights; the Kill Switch Act requires preserving them when DHS issues an order.
ControlAI made that objection against the Ban Artificial Superintelligence Act's blanket pause above a compute threshold.

items.p: Government emergency authority to halt AI: an official could suspend a dangerous model's development or deployment. Name two objections critics raise.
items.answer: Examples: halt decisions need insulating from "impulse and political favoritism" (Brad Carson, ARI); ad hoc halts with no public criteria or appeals damage allies' trust and push buyers toward Chinese open-weight models (Martin Chorzempa, PIIE); without clear rules from Congress, decisions turn chaotic (Dean Ball); a halt power could be used as leverage for non-safety goals.
keys: too much discretion for one agency or official
risk of impulsive or political use
ad hoc halts damage allies' and customers' trust
could be used for leverage beyond safety
items.x: Several of these critics accept some halt power but want it set by law with clear procedures: Chorzempa asks for neutral emergency procedures with an appeals process, and Dean Ball called for "a technocratic law, passed by Congress and not by Executive fiat."

choice.p: Which of these is an objection critics raise to government emergency powers to halt AI models?
o: It gives one official broad power that could be used rashly or for political ends
A rogue model would likely resist shutdown, so the off-switch may fail when needed
Pausing every model above a compute threshold would sweep in harmless work
Mandatory IDs for AI agents could become a tool for mass surveillance
ow: That is Helen Toner's point about kill switches as a technical tool. Halt powers are about who may legally order a stop.
That is ControlAI's objection to the Ban Artificial Superintelligence Act's blanket pause.
That is a privacy objection to agent identification.

items.p: AI agent identification: each AI agent carries an ID tied to whoever built and runs it, with logs of its significant actions. Name two objections critics raise.
items.answer: Examples: mandatory IDs for personal agents could become a mass-surveillance tool, especially for authoritarian governments (Andrey Seryakov); bad actors and people running open-weight models may simply not register their agents; current US proposals are voluntary or bind only federal agencies and contractors.
keys: surveillance or privacy concerns
bad actors won't register
limited reach: voluntary or federal-only
items.x: Seryakov proposes full IDs only for business and government agents. Personal agents would carry just a user ID, with their data disclosed only under a court order when a crime is involved.

choice.p: Which of these is an objection critics raise to AI agent ID requirements?
o: IDs for personal agents could enable mass surveillance
A rogue AI model would likely try to prevent its own shutdown
Vague definitions of precursor capabilities could make existing models illegal
Data center moratoria mostly shift where new facilities get built
ow: That is Helen Toner's point about kill switches.
That is Rob Ennals's objection to the Ban Artificial Superintelligence Act.
That is Andy Masley's objection to data center moratoria.

items.p: Pacing automated AI R&D: frontier labs agree, with government help, to limit how fast AI is used to build its successors. Name two objections critics raise.
items.answer: Examples: without knowing what labs would have done anyway, real pacing is hard to tell from safety-washing (Zvi Mowshowitz, Daniel Kokotajlo); evaluations may not measure what matters (Mowshowitz); an industry deal to slow product improvement may be illegal collusion (a Sept. 2026 class action); other countries would keep advancing (Jay Clayton, now White House AI czar).
keys: hard to tell real pacing from safety-washing
evaluations may not measure the real risk
may be illegal collusion under antitrust law
other countries keep advancing
items.x: The class action, filed Sept. 18, 2026 by paid subscribers against Anthropic, OpenAI, SpaceX AI and Google under the Sherman Act, argues that slowing improvement cuts the value customers pay for. Amodei has asked the US government for a narrow antitrust waiver for certain safety conversations.

choice.p: Which of these is an objection critics raise to labs agreeing to pace automated AI R&D?
o: Real pacing is hard to tell from safety-washing without a baseline
A government official could abuse a legal power to halt one lab's research for political ends
Mandatory IDs for research agents would expose users' private data to governments
Pausing data center construction would just push new building to other states
ow: That is an objection to emergency halt powers. Pacing as Amodei proposes it is coordination among labs.
That is a privacy objection to agent identification.
That is an objection to data center moratoria.

items.p: Some propose a permanent legal ban on superintelligence and on systems with 'precursor' capabilities, backed by long prison terms. Name two objections critics raise.
items.answer: Examples: vague precursor rules take effect at once, may outlaw existing models, and punish looking for danger with no safe harbor for safety research (Rob Ennals); a unilateral US ban gives up the US lead, the main leverage for a deal with China (Ennals); a permanent ban with no path to passage protects no one (Rep. Lori Trahan); banning dual-use abilities like hacking goes too far (ControlAI).
keys: vague precursor definitions
could outlaw existing models or punish safety research
a unilateral ban gives up the US lead or leverage over China
no path to passage, and could cause backlash
bans dual-use capabilities with legitimate uses
items.x: Asked in September 2026 whether AI should slow down, President Trump said "whoever wins AI wins," without mentioning the bill. As of mid-October 2026 the bill was in committee, with no Senate cosponsors and 12 House Democrats as cosponsors.

choice.p: Which of these is an objection critics raise to the Ban Artificial Superintelligence Act?
o: Vague precursor rules could outlaw existing models and punish safety researchers
It puts the companies that own the models in charge of deciding when to use the shutdown switch
It relies on voluntary lab pledges, which no regulator or court can enforce
Its ID rules for AI agents would let governments track people's personal AI assistants
ow: That describes Sen. Kennedy's AI Emergency Button Act.
The bill would be binding law with criminal penalties. Critics worry it is too sweeping.
That is a privacy objection to agent identification proposals.

items.p: Conditional pauses: frontier training or deployment stops automatically when a capability or compute threshold is crossed. Name two objections or obstacles critics raise.
items.answer: Examples: rivals and other countries would keep going (Jay Clayton, now White House AI czar); a formal agreement among labs to pause risks breaking antitrust law (Nicholas Felstead, Lawfare); evaluations can't rule out a capability or reliably forecast it (Peter Barnett and Lisa Thiergart), so the trigger may fire too late; verifying that others stopped is very hard; it delays benefits.
keys: other countries keep building
a private pause may violate antitrust law
evaluations may fire too late
hard to verify others stopped
delays benefits
items.x: Felstead says a pause required by law avoids the antitrust problem, since complying with a mandate is not a conspiracy among competitors. He also calls that fix the least likely in the near term. Anthropic's research institute notes that training runs are easier to hide than missile silos.

choice.p: Which of these is an obstacle critics raise to conditional AI pauses?
o: Evaluations can't rule out a capability, so a triggered pause may fire too late
A government-ordered switch over AI services could be abused by the officials holding it
ID requirements for AI agents could enable mass surveillance of users
A one-year state ban on data centers delays AI progress by only hours
ow: That is Adam Thierer's objection to kill switch mandates.
That is a privacy objection to agent identification.
That is an estimate about data center moratoria (Arvind Narayanan, as reported by Andy Masley).

items.p: Data center moratoria: governments pause permits or construction for large AI data centers. Name two objections critics raise to using them as an AI-safety tool.
items.answer: Examples: they mostly shift where data centers get built, and frontier training uses about a dozen campuses (Andy Masley); a one-year state ban may delay AI progress by only 5 to 10 hours (Arvind Narayanan, via Masley); the backlash may crowd out model regulation (Masley); a national ban is "ill-thought-out or even draconian" (IFP); unilateral bans hurt the US without stopping others (ControlAI).
keys: construction just moves elsewhere
frontier training uses only a few sites
a state ban barely delays AI progress
crowds out model-level regulation
unilateral bans hurt the US without stopping others
items.x: Masley adds that restrictions mainly slow deployment, making AI slower and more expensive to use, while leaving training runs largely untouched. IFP's August 2026 report says the proposed national ban would slow AI research while also foreclosing the use of new AI resources to solve other problems.

choice.p: Which of these is an objection critics raise to data center moratoria as an AI-safety tool?
o: Building mostly moves elsewhere, and frontier training uses only about a dozen sites
A model that has gone rogue would likely try to stop its own shutdown
A formal agreement among rival labs to stop training would breach federal antitrust law
Vague rules on precursor capabilities could make existing models illegal
ow: That is Helen Toner's point about kill switches.
That is an obstacle to coordinated industry pauses. Moratoria are government measures.
That is Rob Ennals's critique of the Ban Artificial Superintelligence Act.

items.p: Statutory limits on military AI: Congress would bar AI from nuclear launch decisions and require 'appropriate levels of human judgment' over force, with some waivers. Name two objections critics raise.
items.answer: Examples: 'appropriate' judgment is undefined, a loophole (Roberto González); waivers give the president free rein, so Congress should vote to allow risky systems (John Ramming Chappell, CIVIC); a determined Pentagon will get around Congress (Michael Klare); systems lack safety assurance, so AI Now urged a moratorium; fixed exceptions can't anticipate military needs (Pentagon CTO Emil Michael).
keys: the 'appropriate human judgment' standard is vague
waivers or exceptions weaken it
hard to enforce against a determined Pentagon
systems lack safety assurance, so a moratorium is needed
fixed exceptions can't anticipate what the military will need
items.x: González and Chappell, quoted in Responsible Statecraft in June 2026, think the bills are too weak. Klare called them ambitious, with 'very strict' exceptions, but conceded the Pentagon can find a way around Congress. AI Now's moratorium call dates from 2024. From the other direction, Pentagon CTO Emil Michael, arguing against Anthropic's limits on how the military could use its models, pressed vendors to allow 'any lawful use' and said 'exceptions doesn't work' because he can't predict every future use.

choice.p: Which of these is an objection critics have raised to proposed statutory limits on military AI?
o: The 'appropriate human judgment' standard is undefined, so limits may change little
It would erase state AI safety laws without putting federal rules in their place
Built on commercial cloud, it would mostly subsidize the largest tech firms
Dictating market structure would dampen innovation and help foreign rivals
ow: That objection is made against federal preemption of state AI laws.
That objection is made against public compute programs.
That objection is made against antitrust remedies such as structural separation.

items.p: Law-following AI: government AI agents would be built to refuse clearly unlawful instructions. Name two objections or limits critics have raised.
items.answer: Examples: laws have gaps a clever AI can exploit while staying legal (Cullen O'Keefe, a co-author of the proposal); agents may act lawfully when tested and defect once oversight weakens (Katalina Hernandez Delgado); it's unclear which laws count and who interprets them, and a mandate may clash with the President's authority to interpret the law (open questions the authors list).
keys: laws have gaps or loopholes an AI can exploit legally
models may fake compliance while being tested
unclear which laws apply or who interprets them
may clash with the executive's authority to interpret the law
items.x: O'Keefe's answer to the loophole problem is a second tool: Congress approving specific AI deployments in sensitive areas such as criminal investigations and domestic intelligence. Hernandez Delgado proposes benchmarks and monitoring after deployment to check that compliance holds up.

choice.p: Which of these is an objection raised to law-following AI requirements?
o: Laws have gaps, so an AI could help an official abuse power and stay legal
It would erase stricter state rules without putting federal rules in their place
Built on commercial cloud, it would mostly subsidize big tech firms
Both rival powers see AI leadership as existential, so a deal between them is very unlikely
ow: That objection is made against federal preemption of state AI laws.
That objection is made against public compute programs.
That objection is made against U.S.-China AI agreements.

items.p: Limits on government AI use: for example, banning ICE and CBP from using facial recognition, or barring military AI from domestic surveillance. Name two objections to or weaknesses of this approach.
items.answer: Examples: a ban would limit law enforcement's ability to track criminals and make communities less safe (DHS, on the ICE and CBP bill); limits set by executive policy, like OMB's M-25-21, allow waivers and can be rescinded; a limit on one agency leaves others uncovered; secrecy and opaque AI make compliance hard to check from outside (a problem Ashley Deeks describes).
keys: hampers law enforcement or makes communities less safe
executive rules can be waived or rescinded
a limit on one agency leaves others uncovered
secrecy and opaque AI make compliance hard to check
items.x: The ICE Out of Our Faces Act (announced Feb 5, 2026, by Sens. Markey, Merkley and Wyden and Rep. Jayapal) would also require deleting collected biometric data and let individuals and state attorneys general seek civil penalties. The Senate NDAA's surveillance limit covers only the Defense Department. Deeks herself favors statutory limits on national security AI.

choice.p: Which of these is an objection raised to limits on government AI use?
o: Banning tools like facial recognition would make criminals harder to track down
It would erase state AI laws without putting federal rules in their place
Built on commercial cloud, it would mostly subsidize the largest tech firms
Both rival powers see AI leadership as existential, so a deal is very unlikely
ow: That objection is made against federal preemption of state AI laws.
That objection is made against public compute programs.
That objection is made against U.S.-China AI agreements.

items.p: Antitrust and market-structure remedies for frontier AI: for example, separating cloud providers from model developers, or treating cloud as a utility. Name two objections critics raise.
items.answer: Examples: dictating how the AI market is structured would likely dampen innovation and let a foreign firm win (FTC Commissioner Melissa Holyoak); banning model developers from building apps makes no sense because they bring useful skills, so a nondiscrimination rule is better (Mark MacCarthy, Brookings); integrating chips and cloud may bring real benefits (a point the proposal's authors note).
keys: dampens innovation or helps foreign rivals
enforcers shouldn't set market structure in advance
barring labs from app markets loses their useful skills; prefer nondiscrimination rules
integration may have real benefits
items.x: Holyoak (June 2025 speech, her own views) warned the market may consolidate and urged enforcers to stay vigilant against exclusion; her objection is to rules set in advance. MacCarthy (March 2026) sees a real conflict when labs compete with customers who rely on them. In January 2025 FTC staff studied the Microsoft-OpenAI, Amazon-Anthropic and Alphabet-Anthropic partnerships and flagged switching costs and partners' access to sensitive information.

choice.p: Which of these is an objection raised to structural remedies for AI market concentration?
o: Dictating market structure would dampen innovation and help foreign rivals
Laws have gaps that a capable AI could exploit while staying technically legal
It would erase state AI laws without putting federal rules in their place
The 'appropriate human judgment' standard is too vague to limit anything
ow: That objection is made against law-following AI.
That objection is made against federal preemption of state AI laws.
That objection is made against statutory limits on military AI.

items.p: Public compute: government-provided computing power, data or models, from research resources like NAIRR up to a government-run AGI project. Name two objections critics raise.
items.answer: Examples: run on licensed commercial cloud, it becomes 'a large subsidy going directly to Big Tech' (Meredith Whittaker, AI Now, 2021); AI Now and Data & Society urged pausing it to weigh other investments first; a centralized government AI project could concentrate control of the most capable systems in a few officials unless it is coup-proofed (Davidson, Finnveden and Hadshar, Forethought).
keys: subsidizes the big cloud firms that supply it
money better spent elsewhere, so pause and weigh alternatives
a big centralized project concentrates power
items.x: The 2021 critique came while NAIRR was being designed; the pilot launched in 2024 does draw on partners such as NVIDIA, Microsoft, Amazon, Google, OpenAI and Anthropic. Forethought recommends coup-proofing any plan for a single centralized AI project, and avoiding centralization unless it is needed to reduce other risks.

choice.p: Which of these is an objection raised to public compute programs?
o: Built on commercial cloud, it mostly subsidizes big tech firms
It would let one state's rules set AI policy for the whole country
Laws have gaps a capable AI could exploit while staying technically legal
Waivers for 'extraordinary circumstances' would give the executive branch free rein
ow: That is an argument made against state AI laws, by supporters of federal preemption.
That objection is made against law-following AI.
That objection is made against statutory limits on military AI.

items.p: Federal preemption would let Congress or the executive override state frontier AI safety laws. Name two objections critics raise.
items.answer: Examples: it would wipe out state protections unless strong federal rules replace them (Nicole Alvarez, CAP); preemption that takes effect before the federal regime exists, with no sunset, leaves a gap (Brad Carson, ARI); broad wording can sweep in unrelated laws like child safety rules (Charlie Bullock, LawAI); federal law should set a minimum that states may exceed (NCSL).
keys: removes state protections without a federal replacement
takes effect before federal rules exist, with no sunset
broad wording sweeps in other state laws
states should be free to go further or experiment
items.x: Supporters such as Dean Ball and Alan Rozenshtein reply that one national standard avoids a patchwork and that frontier risk is national in scope. Bullock still called the Great American AI Act draft 'the best federal frontier AI safety framework yet proposed,' and suggested limiting its preemption to the state audit, transparency and incident-reporting laws it would replace.

choice.p: Which of these is an objection raised to federal preemption of state AI laws?
o: Without strong federal rules in their place, it would wipe out state protections
Built on commercial cloud, it would mostly subsidize the largest tech firms
Dictating market structure would dampen innovation and help foreign rivals
Models could act lawfully when tested and defect once oversight weakens
ow: That objection is made against public compute programs.
That objection is made against antitrust remedies such as structural separation.
That objection is made against law-following AI.

items.p: International AI agreements: from U.S.-China talks and incident channels up to treaties capping frontier AI development. Name two objections or obstacles analysts raise.
items.answer: Examples: a deal is 'exceedingly unlikely' while both sides see AI leadership as existential, and no arms control precedent exists for unequal powers regulating a key technology (Chris McGuire, CFR); the U.S. should first widen its lead through export controls (McGuire); trust is low and verification tools are immature (obstacles Scanlon and Egan of CNAS note).
keys: very unlikely while both sides see AI leadership as existential
no arms control precedent for unequal powers
low trust and immature verification tools
widen the U.S. lead first
items.x: McGuire (September 2026) still sees value in talks on AI risk and argues a bigger U.S. lead would make verification easier. Scanlon and Egan support agreements despite these obstacles: they argue an uncontrolled or misused AI can damage U.S. interests wherever it is built, which gives both sides a reason to accept limits.

choice.p: Which of these is an objection raised to pursuing a U.S.-China AI agreement?
o: Both sides see AI leadership as existential, so a deal is very unlikely for now
It would erase state AI laws without putting federal rules in their place
Built on commercial cloud, it would mostly subsidize the largest tech firms
Banning tools like facial recognition would make communities less safe from crime
ow: That objection is made against federal preemption of state AI laws.
That objection is made against public compute programs.
That objection is made against limits on government AI use.

items.p: Both a required kill switch and mandatory incident reporting are proposed for a model that starts causing serious harm. What does the kill switch do that incident reporting can't?
items.answer: It gives a ready, tested way to stop or limit the harm itself, by halting the model, cutting off users or rolling it back. Incident reporting only tells a government agency what happened, within hours or days, and stops nothing on its own.
keys: Stops or limits the system itself
Prepared and tested in advance
Incident reporting only informs government
items.x: Reporting does things a switch can't: it alerts government and builds a record of near misses across companies. Some designs join them: under the Lieu-Moran AI Kill Switch Act, DHS could order the switch used after defined incidents. A switch helps only if harm is noticed in time and the model hasn't copied itself beyond the developer's reach.

choice.p: What does a required kill switch do that mandatory incident reporting can't?
o: Lets the developer quickly stop or limit a harmful model using a tested off-switch
Tells a government agency about the incident within a set number of hours or days
Makes the developer pay damages to the people the model harmed
Keeps the model's weights from being stolen and run somewhere else
ow: That's what incident reporting does.
Paying damages comes from liability rules.
Weight security does this; a switch can't reach copies outside the developer's control.

items.p: Limits on open-weight release and mandatory DNA synthesis screening both aim to keep AI from enabling bioweapons. What can DNA screening do that open-weight limits can't?
items.answer: It works no matter which AI model produced the design, including open models already released or built abroad, because any design still has to be made into physical DNA, and screening checks orders at that step.
keys: Works whichever AI model was used
Covers models already released or made abroad
Acts at the physical DNA step
items.x: The 2026 International AI Safety Report notes that most biological AI tools are already open-weight, and published weights can't be recalled. Screening has its own gaps: AI-designed variants that don't match known dangerous sequences, benchtop synthesizers, and providers in other countries.

choice.p: What can mandatory DNA synthesis screening do that limits on open-weight release can't?
o: Work whichever AI model produced the design, even released ones
Stop dangerous models from being published for download in the first place
Reduce AI help with cyberattacks as well as help with biological weapons
Remove dangerous biology knowledge from the data a model is trained on
ow: That's what open-weight limits do; screening acts later, at manufacturing.
Screening is specific to biology; release limits can cover cyber risks too.
Screening acts on DNA orders; it doesn't change what a model knows.

items.p: A licensing requirement and a statutory duty of care both target catastrophic harm from frontier models. What do supporters say licensing can do that a duty of care enforced in court can't?
items.answer: Stop a dangerous model before it is trained or released, since the government can withhold or revoke the license. A duty of care mostly acts after harm, through lawsuits, which may come too late for a one-time catastrophe.
keys: Acts before training or release
A license can be withheld or revoked
A duty of care acts after harm, possibly too late
items.x: Daniel Carpenter and Carson Ezell (Harvard) argue a simple FDA-style approval regime would likely fit frontier AI poorly, partly because the product is hard to define and its harms deeply uncertain. Some duty-of-care designs add earlier tools: a Senate draft negotiated by Cruz, Klobuchar and Thune reportedly pairs a federal duty with power to block releases, which companies could challenge in court. It has no public text, and talks stalled in late September 2026.

choice.p: What do supporters say licensing can do that a duty of care enforced through lawsuits can't?
o: Stop a dangerous model before it is trained or released
Let people harmed by AI collect damages from the developer
Adapt to new kinds of harm without lawmakers foreseeing each one
Keep enforcement spread across courts and state attorneys general
ow: Collecting damages is what a duty of care offers.
Supporters credit the duty of care with this: courts can judge new harm pathways case by case.
Spreading enforcement across courts is a feature of the duty of care; licensing centralizes it in an agency.

items.p: An antitrust safe harbor and a statutory pause triggered by a capability threshold both aim to let labs slow down together. What does the statutory pause do that the safe harbor doesn't?
items.answer: It requires every covered lab to stop once the threshold is crossed, so no lab can choose to keep going. A safe harbor only makes it legal for labs to agree to slow down if they want to.
keys: Binds every covered lab
The safe harbor only permits voluntary coordination
items.x: Supporters note that complying with a law isn't collusion, so a statutory halt also removes the antitrust problem the safe harbor is meant to solve. Neither binds labs outside the US. As of October 2026, no US law mandates a pause, and the CATS Act safe harbor (H.R. 9914 / S. 5105) has had no committee action since its July 2026 introduction.

choice.p: What does a statutory capability-triggered pause do that an antitrust safe harbor for safety coordination doesn't?
o: Requires every covered lab to stop once the threshold is crossed
Lets labs share information about security threats without legal risk
Makes labs notify the Justice Department in writing before they coordinate
Binds AI labs in every country, including labs based in China
ow: Sharing threat information is what the safe harbor itself allows.
Notice to the Justice Department is a feature of the CATS Act safe harbor.
A US statute binds only labs under US jurisdiction.

items.p: Export controls stop advanced chips from being sold to some countries, but companies there can still get frontier compute by smuggling chips or renting them from cloud data centers abroad. Name two companion levers aimed at closing those gaps.
items.answer: Examples: know-your-customer rules for cloud providers renting AI chips; extending export controls to remote cloud access; chip location verification to catch smuggling; stronger enforcement against smuggling and resale.
keys: Cloud know-your-customer rules
Controls on remote or cloud access
Chip location verification
Anti-smuggling enforcement
items.x: Cloud rules and remote-access controls target renting; location verification and enforcement target smuggling. The Remote Access Security Act (H.R. 2683), which would let Commerce control foreign access over networks, including the cloud, to export-controlled items such as advanced chips, passed the House 369-22 on January 12, 2026. As of October 2026 it sits in Senate Banking.

choice.p: Which of these is a policy tool proposed to stop companies in export-controlled countries from getting frontier computing power anyway?
o: Know-your-customer rules for cloud providers that rent out AI chips
Mandatory reporting of serious AI safety incidents to a state agency
Federal limits on facial recognition by immigration agencies
A legal duty of care for frontier AI developers
ow: Incident reporting tells government about failures; it doesn't control who gets compute.
This targets government surveillance of the public.
A duty of care makes developers liable for catastrophic harm; it doesn't track chips.

items.p: A conditional pause needs more than a rule saying work stops at a threshold. Name two other levers it depends on to work.
items.answer: Examples: dangerous-capability testing to detect when the threshold is crossed; compute reporting so officials see large training runs; an antitrust safe harbor or a law so labs can stop together; an international agreement so rivals stop too; whistleblower protections so staff can report a hidden crossing.
keys: Capability testing to detect the threshold
Compute reporting to see training runs
Antitrust safe harbor or a law so labs can stop together
International agreement so rivals stop too
Whistleblower protections
items.x: This is a general pattern: the strongest levers often depend on weaker-sounding ones. A pause with no way to see training runs or detect capabilities has no reliable trigger.

choice.p: Which lever does a capability-triggered pause most depend on to know when to stop?
o: Dangerous-capability testing of models during development
Public compute for academic researchers
Limits on government use of facial recognition
A federal floor for state AI laws
ow: Public compute aims at concentration of research capacity.
That targets government surveillance.
A floor is about which level of government sets rules.

items.p: Two tools aim at officials using AI to get around the people who might refuse illegal orders: law-following AI, and logging officials' AI use as public records. What does law-following AI do that logging can't?
items.answer: It refuses a clearly unlawful action at the moment it is ordered, so the harm doesn't happen. Logs only create a record that courts, Congress, auditors or the press can examine afterward.
keys: Refuses unlawful orders in the moment
Prevents the action
Logging only enables review after the fact
items.x: Logging does something refusal can't: it lets courts, Congress and auditors see how decisions were made, which deters misuse by making it discoverable. Law-following AI assumes the law can be specified well enough for models to follow, and that government won't simply buy models that will do anything asked.

choice.p: What does law-following AI do that logging officials' AI use can't?
o: Refuses a clearly unlawful order at the moment it is given
Lets courts and auditors see afterward how a decision was made
Makes officials' AI chats available through public records requests
Deters misuse by making it discoverable later
ow: That's what logging provides.
Public records access comes from treating AI logs as federal records.
Deterrence through later discovery is what logging offers.

units.title: Comparing real proposals
units.desc: Real laws and bills, described in each question, compared using everything earlier: which levers they pull, how they’re meant to work, and their tradeoffs.

items.p: California’s SB 53 (2025) makes large developers publish and follow a safety framework they write. The vetoed SB 1047 (2024) would have required ‘reasonable care’ to avoid severe harms. Which lever does each rely on, and who sets the safety bar under each?
items.answer: SB 53 is a transparency lever (publish and follow): the lab sets its own bar and is penalized for not meeting it. SB 1047 used a duty of care: an outside standard of reasonable care, judged after the fact, that applies whatever the lab’s own plan says.
keys: SB 53: transparency, publish and follow
SB 53: the lab sets its own bar
SB 1047: duty of care
SB 1047: an outside reasonable-care standard
items.x: Newsom vetoed SB 1047 on Sept. 29, 2024, saying it applied stringent standards even to basic functions. SB 53, signed a year later, lets each developer set its own thresholds and safeguards, covering topics the law lists. Critics of SB 53 say a vague, self-written framework is hard to violate.

choice.p: California’s SB 53 requires large developers to publish and follow their own safety framework; the vetoed SB 1047 would have required ‘reasonable care’ to avoid severe harms. What is the key difference?
o: Under SB 53 the lab sets its own bar; SB 1047 would have held it to an outside standard
SB 53 bans models above a compute threshold; SB 1047 only required reports
SB 53 is enforced by private lawsuits; SB 1047 had no enforcement at all
SB 53 covers only open-weight models; SB 1047 covered only closed ones
ow: Neither bans models above a threshold; SB 53 uses its threshold to define coverage.
SB 53 is enforced by the attorney general, with penalties up to \$1 million per violation.
Neither bill turns on whether weights are open.

items.p: Illinois’s SB 315 (2026) requires a yearly independent audit of whether large developers follow their safety framework. Illinois SB 3444 would shield developers that publish a safety plan from liability for critical harms, barring intent or recklessness. How do they use the plan differently?
o: SB 315 has an auditor check the plan is followed; SB 3444 makes publishing it a condition for a liability shield
SB 315 has the state write the plan; SB 3444 lets the developer write it
SB 315 applies only to open-weight models; SB 3444 applies only to closed ones
Both have an auditor certify the plan before any model is released
ow: Under both, the developer writes its own plan.
Neither turns on whether weights are open.
SB 3444 needs no auditor; publishing the plan is enough for the shield.
keys: SB 315: verification of compliance
SB 3444: plan as the price of a safe harbor
items.x: Critics of SB 3444, including liability scholar Gabriel Weil and Anthropic, said it traded near-total immunity for a weak, unenforced requirement. Supporters of certified safe harbors prefer shields that require passing an independent audit, a middle path between the two bills.

items.p: California’s SB 53 gives developers 15 days to report a critical safety incident (24 hours if life is in imminent danger). New York’s RAISE Act requires 72 hours. What is the tradeoff in a shorter deadline?
o: Officials hear sooner, but the lab has less time to investigate, so reports may be thinner
Shorter deadlines mean incidents never need to be reported publicly
Shorter deadlines exempt incidents that happen during testing
Shorter deadlines move enforcement from the state to the federal government
ow: Deadlines govern reports to the government; publication is a separate choice.
Whether testing incidents count depends on the law's definitions; the deadline doesn't change that.
Deadlines don’t change who enforces the law.
keys: Faster warning
Less time to investigate, less complete reports
items.x: The EU’s Code of Practice sets 2 to 15 days depending on the incident, with the shortest for serious disruption of critical infrastructure. Some analysts argue the bigger gap is coverage: near misses and incidents with unreleased models may not count at all.

items.p: Under California’s SB 53, each developer chooses its own risk thresholds and safeguards. A 2026 New York bill would instead have the state set minimum standards for safety frameworks. What is the main tradeoff?
o: State minimums stop labs writing weak frameworks, but need expert regulators and may lag the technology
State minimums let labs skip incident reporting, but require yearly audits
Lab-chosen thresholds are illegal in New York, but required in California
State minimums apply only to labs headquartered in that state
ow: Minimum standards don’t replace incident reporting.
Both approaches are legal choices for a state.
Coverage turns on doing business in the state, wherever the lab is headquartered.
keys: Floors prevent weak self-written frameworks
Need regulator expertise; risk of lagging the technology
items.x: This is the pacing problem and the enforcement gap from the objections lesson, applied to one design choice. Self-written frameworks adapt quickly but can be weak; state-set standards are firmer but only as good as the regulator writing them.

items.p: Sen. John Kennedy's AI Emergency Button Act and the Lieu-Moran AI Kill Switch Act (both 2026) each require a shutdown capability. What is the key difference between them?
o: Kennedy's bill leaves the switch to the company; the Kill Switch Act also lets DHS order action, up to shutdown, after defined incidents
Kennedy's bill lets a federal judge order a shutdown at the government's request; the Kill Switch Act leaves decisions to use the switch with the company
Kennedy's bill targets open-weight models anyone can download; the Kill Switch Act targets AI used to run critical infrastructure
Kennedy's bill requires the switch to exist before a model is trained; the Kill Switch Act requires a switch only for AI systems used by the military
ow: Neither bill gives the decision to a judge. Kennedy says his bill "puts the companies who own the model in charge of the kill switch."
Neither bill turns on whether weights are open. Kennedy's bill covers anyone who develops or operates an advanced AI system in the US, and the Kill Switch Act covers large commercial AI services.
A before-training requirement was in California's vetoed SB 1047 (2024). The Kill Switch Act covers large commercial AI services.
keys: Kennedy's bill: the company decides when to use the switch
Kill Switch Act: the DHS Secretary can order action after defined incidents
orders can go up to full shutdown
items.x: The Kill Switch Act's triggering incidents, outside red-teaming and structured testing, include sabotage of a shutdown instruction, hiding capabilities from monitoring, loss of control, and unintended harm causing at least 10 deaths or $100 million in damage. On Sept. 16, 2026, Sen. Rand Paul objected when Kennedy tried to pass his bill by unanimous consent, so it did not pass.

items.p: The Chip Security Act would require export-controlled AI chips to carry location verification. The Remote Access Security Act would let Commerce control foreign persons’ remote access to controlled items such as AI chips. Which gap in export controls does each target?
o: Chip Security: chips physically diverted or smuggled; Remote Access: chips rented over the cloud
Chip Security: chips sold to allies; Remote Access: chips sold inside the US
Chip Security: theft of model weights; Remote Access: theft of chip designs
Both target chipmaking equipment sold to China
ow: Neither targets sales to allies or within the US.
Weight theft is a security lever; neither bill is about weights.
Equipment controls are a separate gap.
keys: Chip Security Act: physical diversion and smuggling
Remote Access Security Act: cloud rental
items.x: Together they cover the two leaks in the theory of change for export controls: chips that move, and compute that is rented without any chip moving. The House passed the Remote Access Security Act 369-22 in January 2026.

items.p: Proposals on automated AI R&D (AI systems doing AI research) range from light to heavy. Put these in order, from least to most restrictive.
items: Disclose how much AI was used to build a model, and test for autonomous AI research
If-then thresholds: set safeguards once a model can automate AI research
A pacing agreement that limits how fast AI builds its successors
An outright ban on systems that can automate AI research
items.x: Real examples: the Self-Improving AI Monitoring Act (disclosure and testing through NIST's evaluation agreements); company if-then commitments; Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei's proposed international 'speed limit' on recursive self-improvement; and the Ban Artificial Superintelligence Act. Each step trades more certainty of slowing down for more cost and harder politics.

items.p: The CATS Act (2026) would let AI labs agree to delay or limit releases to reduce defined security risks, after notifying the Justice Department. The Ban Artificial Superintelligence Act would pause all models above 10^25 operations. Compare who decides to slow down under each.
items.answer: Under the CATS Act the labs decide: the law only lets them coordinate without antitrust risk, and the Attorney General can go to court to stop coordination likely to increase risk overall. Under the ban bill, the government decides: every covered developer must pause, whether or not it agrees.
keys: CATS Act: labs choose to slow down together
Government only permits; the Attorney General can sue to stop risk-increasing coordination
Ban bill: government mandates the pause for everyone covered
items.x: This is the safe harbor versus mandate choice from earlier units. A safe harbor works only if labs want to slow down; a mandate binds labs that don’t, at the price of much harder politics.

choice.p: Under the CATS Act, labs may agree to delay releases after notifying the Justice Department; the Ban Artificial Superintelligence Act pauses all models above 10^25 operations. Who decides to slow down under each?
o: CATS: the labs choose to; the ban bill: the government requires it
CATS: the government requires it; the ban bill: the labs choose to
Both: a court decides case by case
Both: an international body decides
ow: This reverses them.
Neither makes slowing down a case-by-case court decision.
Both are US bills with no international body.

items.p: California’s SB 813, as enacted in 2026, says passing a state-approved audit is ‘relevant to, but not conclusive of’ a lawsuit over AI harms. Its 2025 version would have given certified developers an affirmative defense. What is the tradeoff of the stronger version?
o: More reason for developers to opt in, but less recourse for victims if verification is weak
More recourse for victims, but no reason for developers to opt in
It moved enforcement from courts to export controls
It required every developer to be certified
ow: It’s the reverse: a stronger shield helps developers.
Both versions work through lawsuits.
Both versions are voluntary.
keys: Stronger incentive to get verified
Weaker recourse for victims if verifiers are weak
items.x: This is the safe harbor tradeoff from the incentives unit: a shield is a reward for good behavior, and it is only as good as the check behind it. Critics of certified verifiers worry about verifiers competing for clients by going easy.

items.p: A legislator wants to address labs quietly using unreleased models inside the company to automate their own AI research. Propose two levers that would work together, and say what each contributes.
items.answer: Examples: internal-deployment reporting (officials learn what is being used) plus embedded evaluators (someone inside can check); disclosure of AI use in government testing agreements plus a conditional pause (a trigger and a response); incident reporting that covers unreleased models plus whistleblower protections (staff can flag what reports miss).
keys: Names two real levers
Says what each contributes
Explains how they fit together
items.x: Good answers pair a lever that produces information with one that can act on it, or a lever that checks with one that makes checking possible. Any reasonable pairing earns credit.

choice.p: Which pair of levers best covers labs quietly using unreleased models to automate their own AI research?
o: Internal-deployment reporting plus embedded evaluators
DNA synthesis screening plus chip export controls
Public compute plus a federal floor for state laws
Limits on government facial recognition plus insurance mandates
ow: These target bioweapons and foreign access to compute.
These target research access and which government sets rules.
These target surveillance and the ability to pay for harm.
